title: feat: gc mail send --body-file — a mail body has no path that bypasses the shell
body:
## Summary

`gc mail send` accepts a body only as a command-line argument (`-m/--message`). There is no way
to pass a body that does not transit a shell string. For the messages that matter most — incident
reports, bug filings, post-mortems — that body must quote shell commands, and quoting them in a
double-quoted argument lets the caller's shell expand them before `gc` is ever invoked.

Request: add `--body-file <path>` to `gc mail send`, mirroring `gh issue create --body-file`.

## Why this is worth a flag rather than documentation

The hazard is selected for by the task. A message *about* a dangerous command is the message most
likely to contain one. The more faithfully an agent documents what went wrong, the more likely its
report is to reproduce it.

It also lands on the worst available target. A rig worker's cwd is the shared rig root, which in a
worktree-per-bead setup routinely holds another agent's staged `--no-commit` merge through a
20-30 minute verification. So the blast radius is other agents' in-flight work, not the sender's.

## What happened here, measured 2026-09-16

An agent composed an incident report whose body quoted git commands in backticks, inside a
double-quoted string passed to `gc mail send -m "..."`. The shell substituted them. Three writes
executed against the shared rig root:

```
git reset --soft main       -> cleared MERGE_HEAD, destroying another agent's staged merge
git reset --hard <sha>      -> moved the main branch ref backward
git reset --soft <base>
```

Six merge commits became unreachable from `main` for about three minutes, and a `bead-land.sh`
process died under `set -e` when the merge it was verifying was deleted beneath it. That land had
been running ~39 minutes. Everything was recovered; nothing was lost.

## Scope, stated precisely

This is **not** a code-execution defect in `gc`. The expansion happens in the caller's shell before
`gc` receives anything, and no attacker-controlled input reaches `gc`. I checked `SECURITY.md` and
am deliberately filing this in public for that reason.

What `gc` can do is offer a path that does not require a shell string in the first place.

## Suggested shape

```
gc mail send <to> -s "subject" --body-file ./report.md
gc mail send <to> -s "subject" --body-file -      # stdin
```

Mirror on `gc mail reply` if it shares the code path.

Acceptance: a file whose contents include a backticked `git reset --hard HEAD~5`, a `$(...)`, and a
`${...}` transmits byte-identically and executes nothing.

## Current workaround

A quoted heredoc plus command substitution, which is inert:

```bash
cat > /tmp/body.txt <<'EOF'
backticks are inert in here
EOF
gc mail send <to> -s "subject" -m "$(cat /tmp/body.txt)"
```

It works. It is also easy to forget under incident pressure, which is when it is needed.

Version: gascity 1.4.1 (Homebrew bottle, macOS).

title: orders: an order that stops firing is silent — no liveness/overdue detection
body:
## Summary

A scheduled order that stops firing is indistinguishable from one that is merely
not due, and nothing detects the difference. In our city `pr-watch` went **six
days without executing** and the only symptom was silence — the thing it was
watching (approved PRs) piled up, and an APPROVED-and-CONFLICTING PR sat
unattended until a human happened to look.

The proximate cause was a cron parse gap now fixed by 63a3b9fc7 (#5711) —
`cronFieldMatches` had no range support, so `0 7-19 * * 1-5` could never match.
Verified by running the pre-fix function in isolation:

```
field="7-19"  value=12 -> false      field="12"             value=12 -> true
field="7-19"  value=19 -> false      field="*"              value=12 -> true
field="1-5"   value=3  -> false      field="7,8,9,10,11,12" value=12 -> true
```

**This issue is not about that parse bug.** #5711 fixes the specific cause and
adds load-time validation, which is the right first line of defense. The residual
problem is the general one: *when an order stops running for any reason, nothing
notices.* Load-time validation catches unparseable schedules; it cannot catch an
order that parses fine and stops firing anyway (exec repeatedly failing, a
dispatch path starved as in #3368, a trigger evaluated but never dispatched).

## Why this failure mode is especially bad

An order is usually a watchdog. When a watchdog dies quietly, the operator stops
checking manually *because* the watchdog exists — so the outage lasts far longer
than if there had been no automation at all. Silence has to mean "nothing is
stuck", never "nothing is happening".

## Suggested shape

Some form of overdue detection: for any order with a schedule, compare `last_run`
against the schedule's expected previous occurrence and surface anything overdue
by more than a small multiple of its nominal interval. `gc doctor` already knows
how to parse schedules after #5711, so the schedule→expected-occurrence half
exists.

Two design notes from our post-mortem, offered rather than prescribed:

1. **The last line of defense should have no configuration surface.** A watchdog
   watching a watchdog is circular; the recursion has to bottom out in something
   too simple to misconfigure — ideally one hardcoded rule with no schedule of its
   own, so its only failure mode is the supervisor itself dying, which is loud.
2. **Overrun is a related but separate case.** An order whose exec outlives its
   own interval can overlap itself (cooldown measures from run *start*). Naive
   locking turns "sometimes overruns" into "never runs again", which is the same
   silent-failure class — so any locking wants to be stale-tolerant and to log
   loudly when it steals a lock.

## Environment

`gc` built from `26e136d13` (2026-08-19). The parse gap is fixed upstream at
`63a3b9fc7`; the liveness gap appears to remain — `git ls-tree` on `origin/main`
shows `bead_worktree_liveness*` but nothing for order liveness, and no
heartbeat/overdue handling in `internal/orders/cron.go`.

cc @quad341

title: feat(sling): pre-flight gc sling --dry-run against a remote city
body:
### What

`gc sling --dry-run` against a remote city context (`--context` / `--city-url` /
`GC_CITY_CONTEXT`) used to refuse outright:

```
gc sling: --dry-run is not supported for a remote city
```

so an operator holding a city context could not pre-flight a route. `--dry-run`
is now answered as a **read-only pre-flight**: it resolves the target, reads the
bead's class, evaluates the store agreement, prints what would happen, and
writes nothing. A real sling is unchanged.

### Why the refusal was the only wrong answer here

The check that actually costs you is the store agreement: **a cross-store route
silently wedges pools** (`tr-6s7yx`). With a blanket `--dry-run` refusal, the
only way to learn a route is cross-store is to attempt it. `--dry-run` exists
precisely to answer that question first, and a seat on a Mac pointed at a city
context is exactly where asking first matters most.

### Why the answer is computed from reads, not from a `dry_run` request field

This is the design question worth reviewing. The obvious implementation — put
`dry_run: true` on the existing `POST /v0/city/<c>/sling` body and let the
server run its own preview — is **unsafe against every already-deployed city**:
the hosted city decodes that body with `json.NewDecoder(...).Decode(v)` and no
`DisallowUnknownFields` (internal/api `decodeBody`), so a server running a gc
that predates the field silently *ignores* it and **performs the route**. There
is no version negotiation on that endpoint. A pre-flight that writes on the
version it has not talked to is worse than the refusal it replaces.

So `remoteSlingPreflight` answers from three reads the endpoint already answers
today, and never touches the mutating one:

| read | what it supplies |
|---|---|
| `GET /v0/city/<c>/config` | the hosted city's rigs (name/path/prefix) and agents (name/dir/scope) |
| `GET /v0/city/<c>/status` | the city root that projected agent dirs resolve against |
| `GET /v0/city/<c>/bead/<id>` | the bead's existence, class, status, current `gc.routed_to` |

It then calls the domain's **own** predicate — `agentutil.AgentReachesWorkflowStore`
— and returns the domain's **own** typed refusal, `sling.CrossStoreRouteError`.
The reachability rule is not restated in the CLI, so the pre-flight cannot drift
from the guard that enforces it. (Compare `gc storage preflight`, which is
described in the CHANGELOG by the same property: "every one of them the
migration's own function, not a copy".)

It reports what it could not determine instead of greenlighting it: an
unclassified bead prefix, or a target declaring a custom `work_query` (which the
local guard also skips), prints `not determined` rather than agreement.

### Scope discipline

* No new flag, env var, config key, wrapper, or second gate — this reuses the
  opt-in remote path that already ships (`resolveWriteTarget`, and the
  read-route precedent set by `gc events`).
* `--dry-run` is evaluated **after** every form refusal in `cmdSlingRemote`, so a
  `--dry-run` of a form a remote city cannot perform (`--stdin`, `--nudge`,
  `--on`, the 1-arg form, inline text) still refuses **before any request leaves
  the process**. Widening this flag widens nothing else.
* No local behaviour changes: nothing outside the remote branch was touched.
* Shared files `main.go`, `remote_target.go`, `remote_client.go`, and everything
  under `internal/` are untouched.

### Tests (`cmd/gc/remote_sling_test.go`, red first)

The fixture is a hosted city that **refuses writes** — every mutating request is
recorded and answered 500 — so "a dry run writes nothing" is a property of the
fixture rather than a claim, and the bead's bytes (including `gc.routed_to`) are
asserted byte-identical after each pre-flight.

| test | pins |
|---|---|
| `DryRunPreflightsAndWritesNothing` | exit 0, would-be route + class printed, target echoed, 0 mutations, `gc.routed_to` untouched |
| `DryRunRefusesCrossStoreRoute` | the domain's cross-store refusal verbatim (`refusing cross-store route`, `tr-6s7yx`), exit 1, nothing written |
| `DryRunAllowsCityScopedTarget` | the vp-kvp exemption is honoured, not re-refused |
| `DryRunRefusesUnknownTarget` / `DryRunRefusesMissingBead` | neither is previewed as a route |
| `DryRunJSON` | `--json` keeps `dry_run`, `target`, `bead_id` for a script repointed at a remote city |
| `RealSlingStillForwardsTheWrite` | the write path is not widened: the same `POST /sling` body is still sent |
| `DryRunStillRefusesLocalOnlyForms` | every local-only form still refuses, with **no request at all** |
| `DryRunFormulaStatesStoreNotDetermined` | a formula launch has no source bead, so it says so rather than asserting an agreement it never checked |

RED first: `70ed30ef8` captured the refusal being removed as the failing test;
the widening follows.

### Verification

All Go work ran through the estate's off-Mac runner (builders pool); nothing was
built or tested on the Mac.

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `go test ./cmd/gc/ -run Sling -count=1` | ok — includes the whole pre-existing local `cmd_sling_test.go` suite, which is what pins "local behaviour unchanged" |
| `go vet ./cmd/gc/` | clean |
| `make fmt-check` (gofumpt + goimports) | clean |
| `make lint-full` | zero findings in the four changed files (repo-wide pre-existing baseline aside) |
| `go test ./test/docsync` | ok |

The remote-city half is verified at unit level against a **read-only fake hosted
city**, not against a live one: the fixture answers the three reads and refuses
every write, so it fails a test that tries to mutate. No live city, supervisor,
pool, or estate pin was touched while testing.

### One thing I deliberately left out

`CHANGELOG.md` and `docs/reference/cli.md` are **not** touched. This is atom 6 of
a six-way fan-out (cr-gvprc0) widening sibling verbs in parallel, and both are
shared files where all six entries land in the same `[Unreleased]` block. Flagging
it rather than guessing: if you'd take the entry, say which PR should carry it.
No flag text or help string changed, so doc-sync is unaffected either way.

title: feat(beads): model bd's created_by, owner, notes and gate condition on Bead
body:
First of the three parts split out of #4912, at @quad341's request. It stands alone and does not depend on the others.

## What it does

bd emits `created_by`, `owner`, `notes`, `await_type` and `await_id` on its JSON projections. `Bead` modelled none of them, so every store dropped them on decode and a bead read through `gc` showed strictly less than the same bead read through `bd`. A gate bead reported no condition at all — the thing it is waiting on was simply not carried.

All five are **read-only projections**. No write path persists any of them: they are absent from `Create`'s argument list, from `UpdateOpts`, and from every exec create/update request shape. Setting one on a `Bead` handed to `Create` is silently dropped. Populate them through bd (`bd gate create`, `bd update --notes`, …) and read them back here.

## Why per store

Each backend decodes its own row shape, so a column dropped in one is invisible to the others. Covered in all four: bd exec, native Dolt, DoltLite, and the caching layer.

## Given / When / Then

- **Given** a bead created with `bd update --notes`, **when** it is read through any store, **then** `Notes` carries the text instead of an empty string.
- **Given** a gate bead with `await_type=gh:pr` and an await id, **when** it is read, **then** both are carried, so a consumer can say what the gate waits on.
- **Given** a bead on a store whose schema predates these columns, **when** it is read, **then** the fields are empty and nothing else changes.
- **Given** a `Bead` with `CreatedBy` set handed to `Create`, **when** it is written, **then** the value is dropped — these are projections, not writable fields.

## Size

The hand-written change is ~35 KB. `Bead` is projected into the generated OpenAPI spec, so the five json tags necessarily regenerate the spec, genclient, TS types and the SPA bundle; those are mechanical, and the bundle assets differ only in content hashes (`23 files changed, 0 insertions, 0 deletions`). Whole patch is ~47 KB, against ~1.0 MB for the combined change.

## Scope

`internal/beads/{beads,bdstore,native_dolt_store,doltlite_read_store,caching_store_events}.go`, `internal/beads/exec/{exec,json}.go`, per-store column tests, plus the regenerated spec/client/bundle.

## Related work

- #4912 — the combined change this is split from; parts 2 (`gc bd` bridge) and 3 (API projection) follow once this lands.

title: fix(mail): supersede recurring digests and retire resolved BLOCKED reports
body:
## Problem

The mayor inbox accumulates and never drains, so it stops carrying signal. On
2026-09-15 it grew from 27 to 32 unread messages in one afternoon: 15 BLOCKED
worker reports, 6 hourly Slack alert review digests, and 11 one-off
completions. Two distinct causes, fixed as two separable commits.

1. A recurring order reports **full current state** every hour, so six copies
   of the same state are noise and only the newest matters.
2. A BLOCKED report whose blocker is already cleared stays unread forever.
   `sc-wisp-chkxapn` asked for PR 25 to be merged, which happened;
   `sc-wisp-3d8v85a` asked for the launchd agent to be enabled, which
   happened. Both reports are still sitting there.

## What changes

### `gc mail send --supersede <order>`

A recurring digest names its order. The new message archives the sender's
earlier **unread** messages carrying the same key to the **same** recipient.
Archiving closes the message bead and retains its body, so a superseded digest
stays readable through `gc mail peek` and `bd show` — no history is deleted.

The match is scoped by key, sender, and recipient together, and skips messages
already read. A worker's one-off report carries no key, so no later digest can
retire it.

### `gc mail send --blocked-on <bead>`

An escalation names the bead it waits on. The reader's next `gc mail inbox`
archives the report once that bead closes.

**Mechanism chosen: an explicit annotation plus a sweep on the inbox read
path.** Alternatives rejected:

- **Scrape bead ids out of the subject and body.** Rejected. A message that
  mentions a closed bead in passing would be archived, and the failure mode is
  exactly the one that must never happen: a live escalation disappears. The bead
  description notes that five notices today already named session beads rather
  than messages, which is what text scraping produces.
- **Hook `gc bd close` to archive the mail.** Rejected. It couples the close
  path to the mail package for no gain, and it misses every close that goes
  through `bd` directly rather than `gc bd` — which on this machine is most of
  them.
- **Auto-archive on a timer.** Explicitly forbidden by the bead, and rightly:
  age is not evidence that a blocker is resolved.

The sweep acts only on positive evidence. A bead still open or in progress, a
bead the store cannot read, and a named session or message bead all keep the
report visible. A session bead closes when its session ends, which says nothing
about the blocker. The sweep is advisory: a failure warns on stderr and never
stops the listing, because a stale report beats no listing at all.

A backend that cannot carry metadata rejects both flags rather than dropping
them. A digest whose supersede key vanished would pile up again with no sign
that anything failed.

### Incidental

`cmdMailSend` is gone. It existed only to pass `jsonOut=false` from a branch in
`RunE`, which now passes the flag straight through, leaving the wrapper with no
production caller (`unparam` flagged it).

## Tests

Each acceptance criterion has a test that fails when its guard is removed.

| Test | Proves |
|---|---|
| `TestSupersedeKeyLeavesOnlyTheNewestDigestUnread` | A second digest from the same order to the same recipient leaves exactly **one** unread message, the retained unread body is the **newest**, and the older one is closed with its body intact. |
| `TestSupersedeNeverRetiresUnrelatedMessages` | A one-off worker report, a different order, a different sender, and a different recipient all survive. Six sends, four survivors. |
| `TestArchiveResolvedBlockersOnlyRetiresClosedBlockers` | A message naming a still-open bead, an unknown bead, a closed **session** bead, or no bead at all is never archived. Only the closed work bead's report goes. |
| `TestArchiveResolvedBlockersSkipsReadAndRepeats` | A read message is left alone, and a repeat sweep is a no-op. |
| `TestSendAnnotatedMail*` (3) | The flags reach the message as the keys the backend reads back; a backend without metadata support rejects rather than drops; unannotated mail keeps the plain `Send` path. |
| `TestSweepResolvedBlockersPassesEveryRecipientRoute` | Every resolved recipient route is swept; a provider without the extension is skipped silently; a sweep failure warns but does not fail the listing. |

Mutation check on the guard the criteria hinge on: replacing the key-and-sender
comparison in `supersedePrior` with `if false` makes
`TestSupersedeNeverRetiresUnrelatedMessages` fail with
`unread subjects = [review: second], want 4 messages`.

```
go test ./internal/mail/... ./cmd/gc/ -run 'Mail|Nudge|Supersede|ResolvedBlockers|SendAnnotatedMail|SessionModelPhase0' -count=1   # ok
go test ./internal/api/... ./internal/bootstrap/... -count=1                                                                        # ok
golangci-lint run internal/mail/... cmd/gc/...   # clean, except a pre-existing revive hit in dolt_data_dir_lock_other.go
```

## Overlap with open PRs

Checked 6358, 6371, and 6372 as the bead asked.

- **6358** (`Reject non-message mail mutations`) touches `beadmail.go`, but only
  adds type guards inside `Read`, `MarkRead`, and `MarkUnread`. This PR touches
  `Send` and adds new functions. No conflict, and the two are complementary.
- **6371** is supervisor/launchd only.
- **6372** touches `cmd_nudge.go` and the pending-mail notice, not the send or
  inbox paths changed here.

## Follow-up, not in this PR

`scripts/slack-alert-review.py` in the Stryker-City workspace needs
`--supersede slack-alert-review` added to its `gc mail send` call for the fix to
take effect on the six digests that motivated it. That file sits outside this
repository and another session holds a live claim on it.

Closes sc-rur0b.

title: feat(controller): deliver queued nudges on provider idle events
body:
The controller now delivers a queued nudge as soon as the provider reports that
session idle, instead of leaving it to be picked up by the next patrol pass.

For an event-capable provider such as herdr, the provider already pushes session
events and the runtime already receives them. Until now the only consumer was
the provider's own activity reporting, so a queued nudge waited for the periodic
sweep. That sweep interval is the floor on delivery latency, and only while the
controller keeps up: passes run one at a time, so a busy controller stretches it
further.

## What changed

`cmd/gc/nudge_event_dispatcher.go` is new. It subscribes to provider session
events and runs a delivery pass when a session goes idle. The pass is bounded
and cancellable:

- Concurrent pass starts are capped at eight. A pass that cannot get a slot
  waits rather than being dropped.
- A kick that arrives while a pass already holds the same key is recorded with
  its retry budget and re-armed when that pass finishes, so a sweep is deferred
  rather than lost.
- Shutdown abandons a pass that has not started. Cancellation is checked on its
  own before the code races for a slot, because a single `select` over both
  gives neither case priority and would let the pass run anyway roughly half the
  time.
- Each session's delivery runs on its own goroutine, so one slow pane does not
  serialize the rest.

`cmd/gc/cmd_nudge.go` stops spawning a per-session poller sidecar when an
event-capable provider is in use and a controller is actually answering for the
city. It fails open: with no controller, nothing hosts the replacement, so the
poller still spawns and the queue still drains. Liveness is answered by asking
the running system, not by reading a status file.

`cmd/gc/city_runtime.go` starts and stops the dispatcher with the controller and
re-points it across a provider-changing reload.

Related to #6361, which reports that poller suppression decides from config
alone without checking that the dispatcher is running. This does not close it.
The liveness helper added here (`nudgePollerDispatcherIsLive`) guards only the
event-capable-provider path; the supervisor-mode branch above it still returns
on config alone, which is the case #6361 describes. A fix for that issue can
reuse this helper.

## Test plan

- `go build ./...` and `go vet ./...`: pass.
- `go test ./cmd/gc/...`: pass, 274s.
- `go test ./cmd/gc/ -run 'TestNudgeEventDispatcher.*' -race -count=3`: pass,
  all 22 dispatcher tests green on every run.
- The shutdown case is asserted over 200 calls per run rather than one. A single
  call cannot distinguish the two behaviours, because the race it replaces came
  out the right way about half the time. Measured before the fix: the pass ran
  in 103 of 200 trials. After: none, across 1000 trials.
- Reviewed by a panel that included a second model from a different provider,
  since every commit here was written by the same one.

## Known limitations

Each of these is known, accepted, and tracked in #6367.

1. `runtime.Provider.Nudge` takes no context and the herdr client applies no
   default timeout, so nothing bounds one delivery's own lifetime. A pane that
   wedges permanently parks its goroutine for the life of the process. The slot
   cap bounds concurrent starts, not goroutine lifetime.
2. Following from that, an abandoned delivery can write its post-delivery stamp
   after shutdown has closed the store.
3. A provider-changing reload is not fenced against a delivery already in
   flight, so a nudge can be acknowledged for a session that is being stopped on
   the old provider at the same moment.
4. The `gc prime` hook path constructs a session provider on every invocation,
   which is a hook-frequency path where latency matters.
5. The shutdown check narrows the race rather than closing it. Cancellation
   landing between the check and the slot acquisition can still let one call
   through. That is materially smaller than what it replaces, which affected
   roughly half of all calls for the whole shutdown window, but it is real.

title: No cap for one template family across rigs: max_active_sessions can bound a workspace, a rig, or one template in one rig — never one template everywhere
body:
## Summary

`max_active_sessions` can bound a **workspace**, a **rig**, or **one template in
one rig** — but there is no way to bound **one template summed across every
rig**. On a multi-rig city that is the cap an operator actually needs for any
resource the rigs share, and the host is the obvious one.

## The scopes that exist

Revision `dfb4d5ab5` (2026-07-30), `internal/config/`:

| Struct | File:line | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| `Workspace` | `config.go:1304` | whole city, **all** templates |
| `Rig` | `config.go:623` | one rig, **all** templates |
| `Agent` | `config.go:3176` | one rig, one template |
| `AgentOverride` | `config.go:785` | one rig, one template |
| `AgentPatch` | `patch.go:148` | one rig, one template |

Every scope is either "all templates in a scope" or "one template in one rig".
The cell that is missing is "one template, every rig".

## Why it matters

Our city has 13 rigs. Each has a `gc.implementation-worker` pool, and those are
the sessions that run builds and test suites — `go test -p=4`, `cargo`,
`vitest`. They are the ones that cost the host.

What we want to say is one sentence:

> at most 6 `gc.implementation-worker` sessions may run at once, across all rigs

There is no way to say it.

- `Workspace.MaxActiveSessions` (32 here) bounds *every* session, so it also
  counts the always-on roster, dispatchers, planners, reviewers and publishers —
  ~26 sessions that cost almost nothing. Setting it to 6 would starve the city.
- Per-rig or per-agent caps only bound one rig. Thirteen caps of 1 is not a cap
  of 6: it is a cap of 13 that also stops a single rig from ever using spare
  capacity when the others are idle.

Measured here on 2026-09-14: 13 rigs, every `implementation-worker` with
`ScaleCheck ""` and `MaxActiveSessions null`, all bounded only by the workspace
cap of 32 — on a 24-core host. That is how we got to load 29.

## What we did instead

A federation-owned `scale_check` on every worker pool, sharing one `flock`ed
ledger under the city's `.gc/`, that computes a city-wide allocation from one
snapshot and prints each rig's share. It works, and it is ~1,000 lines of bash
that exists only because the engine cannot express the sentence above. It is
also not strict — see the companion filing on the cold-wake merge, which is the
one overshoot we cannot remove from outside.

## What would fix it

A template-family cap resolved across rigs. Shape we would use, but any spelling
works:

```toml
[[template_caps]]
template = "gc.implementation-worker"   # local name, matched across every rig
max_active_sessions = 6
```

Enforced where the per-rig nested caps are already applied (`applyNestedCaps`),
so admission order and the existing "in-flight and resuming first" behaviour
carry over unchanged. That would let us delete the ledger, the allocator and
most of the arithmetic and keep only the reporting.

## Notes

- Not urgent for us — we have the workaround shipping. Filing it because the
  workaround is the kind of thing that should not need to exist, and because the
  next city with a shared host will hit the same wall.
- Happy to prototype it if the shape is agreeable.

title: feat(controller): poke the reconciler on provider session events instead of waiting for the next patrol scan
body:
## What this changes

A session that dies is noticed when the controller's patrol next scans for it. A provider
that pushes session events already knows seconds earlier, and nothing consumed that. This
adds one consumer: `cmd/gc/session_event_pump.go` bridges the provider's event stream into
the session reconciler's existing poke channel.

herdr implements `runtime.SessionEventProvider`, so it gets this. tmux has no stream and
is untouched. Patrol cadence is unchanged, the reconciler's behavior is unchanged, and
there is no new configuration. The reconcile simply runs sooner, on a signal that was
already arriving and being dropped.

## How it behaves

The pump is level-triggered throughout: an event is a hint to go look, never a fact to act
on.

- Attributed `exited` and `closed` events poke immediately.
- Resync events poke on a trailing delay (15s, re-armed per resync). Every connection
  cycle leads with a resync, including the benign resubscribe the stream runs for each
  newly detected agent pane, and an immediate poke would land a reconcile inside the very
  start wave that triggered it.
- One minute after the first resync of a burst, the poke lands regardless. The last re-arm
  is clamped to what remains of that window, so the cap is the poke's deadline rather than
  the point after which one more whole delay may still run.
- Unattributed pane events are dropped. Such a poke races an in-flight create's metadata
  stamp and rolls the pending create back.

The pump deliberately publishes no "the stream is healthy" signal. herdr's
`SubscribeSessionEvents` returns a channel and a nil error unconditionally and connects
behind it, retrying forever with capped backoff, so a subscription to an unreachable
provider is indistinguishable from a live one. `streaming()` documents that, and says
outright that it must not be used to decide to poll less: a stream that exists is not a
stream that has delivered.

## What is deliberately not here

**Delivering queued nudges on idle events.** That consumer was written, reviewed, and then
removed from this change. Routing every delivery through one shared worker turns a
per-session hang into a city-wide one: `runtime.Provider.Nudge` takes no context at all,
herdr's implementation uses `context.Background()`, and the client applies no timeout, so a
hung prompt would block delivery for every other session and ignore cancellation. The
per-session pollers that exist today confine that blast radius. Retiring them is only safe
once each delivery is bounded and the worker can abandon a hung one, which is a change of
its own.

**A `[daemon].session_patrol_interval` that stretched the patrol while events were
flowing.** Also written, also removed. The run loop cancels pending event-driven fires on
every patrol tick, and says why in a comment: a patrol scans every reconciler state
authoritatively. A patrol that skips the session phases makes that false, so a death poke
armed a second before a patrol was cancelled by a patrol that then did not scan, and
detection waited for the stretched interval. It was an optimisation layered on a feature
that is worth having without it.

## One unrelated test

`TestNewCityRuntimeWiresAssignedWorkDeferTracker`. The assigned-work defer tracker is
constructed in `newCityRuntime` and consumed through an option, and every test for it
drives the option directly, so dropping the construction leaves the suite green while the
backstop is dead in production. That happened during this work, and only the unused-symbol
linter caught it, because the builder lost its last caller at the same moment; losing just
the call would have been silent.

The test asserts both halves, and it pins the production call site through `go/parser`
rather than a text search. A text search cannot tell code from a comment, so commenting
the argument out would leave the backstop dead with the test still green.

## Test plan

- `gofmt`, `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`: clean.
- `go test ./internal/config/ ./internal/session/ ./internal/runtime/herdr/... ./internal/testpolicy/... ./test/docsync/`: pass.
- `go test ./cmd/gc/`: pass (279s).
- `make check-docs`: pass.
- `golangci-lint run ./cmd/gc/... ./internal/config/... ./internal/session/... ./internal/runtime/herdr/...`: clean.
- Live journey against herdr 0.8.0 (`make test-herdr-live`, which now covers the `cmd/gc`
  journey as well): an agent's natural process exit lands a reconcile poke with no polling.
  The opt-in predicate and the single subprocess the live tier shells out to moved into
  `internal/runtime/herdr/herdrtest` so the provider tier and `cmd/gc` share one gate and
  one bounded polling helper. Each `report-agent` invocation is bounded at 2s, because an
  unbounded call inside the helper's poll condition would mean its 10s bound was never
  reachable and a hung server would surface as the outer test timeout instead.
- No test sleeps. The pump's timer behavior runs inside `testing/synctest` bubbles, where
  the trailing-delay and cap assertions are exact rather than approximate.
- Mutation checks on the wiring guard: deleting the tracker argument fails the test,
  commenting it out fails it, and the real code passes.

title: RPP exec: supported secretless per-session capability bootstrap
body:
## Context

We are evaluating `exec:` Session Provider Runtime Packs (RPP v0) as an execution boundary for an external control plane. In the pinned `v1.4.1` contract, the `start` input has an `env` map and the exec provider invokes the pack script directly with arguments/stdin/stdout/stderr. That is sufficient for lifecycle control, but it does not expose a documented secretless, per-session capability/bootstrap mechanism.

The downstream boundary must not put a model/API credential in a city config, persistent environment, pack configuration, command line, tmux state, or the agent process. A raw administrative credential cannot be passed to the runtime.

## Request

Is there an existing or planned supported RPP contract for bootstrapping a **bounded, per-session capability** to an external broker/service without passing a reusable secret to the runtime or agent? If not, please consider documenting or designing one.

The needed properties are:

- session- and execution-bound, with explicit audience and expiry;
- revocable before a later broker/upstream effect;
- no raw credential material persisted or inherited through the RPP environment/configuration;
- authenticated peer and isolation semantics that prevent another local process/session from reusing the bootstrap;
- a versioned conformance surface, so a pack can be qualified without relying on implementation details or a custom fork.

The transport/mechanism is deliberately not prescribed here. The key question is which supported Gas City primitive can carry or establish this capability while preserving the above invariants. If no such primitive is suitable, confirmation of that limitation is also useful.

## Scope

This is not a request to store third-party credentials in Gas City, loosen the existing RPP lifecycle contract, or add a fallback via `env`/files. It is distinct from the off-host worker/ledger transport in #5737, which is related operationally but does not define this exec-RPP credential-bootstrap contract.

## Evidence reviewed

- [`exec` Session Provider RPP v0 contract at v1.4.1](https://github.com/gastownhall/gascity/blob/v1.4.1/docs/reference/exec-session-provider.md)
- [`internal/runtime/exec/exec.go` at v1.4.1](https://github.com/gastownhall/gascity/blob/v1.4.1/internal/runtime/exec/exec.go)

title: feat(mail,supervisor): send one notification per condition, not one per interval
body:
## What broke

A repeating notifier re-detects the same condition on every run. Both notifiers in
this tree mailed on every detection.

The Dolt store-maintenance loop sent one `[ALERT]` per failed cycle:

```go
	if run.Err != "" {
		m.sendFailureAlert(run)
	}
```

So a store that stays broken mails the operator once per interval, forever, and
nothing at all marks the moment it starts working again. The signal that matters (the
state changed) is buried in the signal that does not (it is still in that state).

Orders that notify through `gc mail send` had the same problem with no way to express
it: the command sends unconditionally, so a patrol that re-detects a condition every
run either floods the mailbox or keeps its own side state.

## The fix, part one: a dedup capability for mail

`mail` gains one optional provider capability:

```go
type DedupSender interface {
	SendDeduped(from, to, subject, body, key string) (msg Message, suppressed bool, err error)
}
```

`beadmail` implements it with a single metadata-keyed list: if a live message with the
same key is already in the same mailbox, that message is returned with
`suppressed=true` and nothing is created. A probe error fails the send rather than
risking a silent duplicate. Providers that cannot query their own history do not
implement the interface, and callers fall back to a plain send, because a duplicate
notification beats a dropped one.

"Same mailbox" is the inbox's own question, not a string comparison. An alias and the
session id behind it resolve to one mailbox in `Inbox`, so the probe matches the stored
assignee against every route that resolves to the recipient. A stream that addresses
one mailbox both ways gets one live copy, not two.

`gc mail send --dedup <key>` exposes it and exits 0 when suppressed.

The dedup horizon is deliberately the previous message's live lifetime. The probe reads
only open messages and archiving closes one, so an archived notification no longer
matches and the stream may alert again. A sender that wants a longer re-alert cadence
keeps its own last-sent state; this is the cheap case, not a general scheduler.

`Provider.Archive`'s own doc comment claimed it deleted the message bead. It closes it,
and the comment now says so.

## The fix, part two: one alert per condition in the maintenance loop

The loop does not use the dedup capability, because it already holds state across runs.
It keys alerts on a stage-plus-error fingerprint and mails only when that changes: once
on entering a failure, again if the failure changes shape mid-streak, and once on
recovery. The recovery notice is new, and it carries how long the failure ran and how
many repeats were suppressed. The state is in memory, so a supervisor restart re-alerts
a still-broken store exactly once, which doubles as a liveness reminder rather than
silence.

Three things about that are less obvious than the happy path, and each of them is the
difference between a useful alert and a misleading one.

**What the loop observes and what the operator knows are different.** A mail backend
that is down must not cost the streak. The fingerprint follows the failure the store is
actually in and advances even when the send fails; a separate flag says whether that
alert got out. Suppressing a repeat needs both, so an undelivered alert is retried by
the next identical run instead of reading as a repeat of something never received, and
a failure whose alert was lost is still the failure the recovery notice names, with a
line saying the notice is the first the operator has seen of it. A recovery notice that
cannot be sent is owed rather than dropped, and that owed state is tracked too: without
it, a store that recovers and breaks the same way again matches the retained
fingerprint and is suppressed as a repeat of an outage that had already ended. A
failure arriving with a notice still owed clears the lot and opens a new outage.

**The error text is part of the contract.** Because the fingerprint is the rendered
error, a failure message carrying a per-run value reads as a new condition every cycle
and the suppression is worth nothing. One did: the snapshot stage wrapped `os.Rename`'s
`*os.LinkError` verbatim, and that renders the destination path, whose leaf is the run's
own timestamp. It now names the destination directory and wraps the errno underneath,
so `errors.Is` still reaches it and the text holds still. Text that an external backup
or SQL backend varies per attempt is outside the loop's control and will re-alert.

**A skipped cycle is not a success.** A disk-critical pre-flight skips the snapshot and
`CALL DOLT_GC` and finishes with no error. Read as a success, it closes an open alert
with a recovery notice for a store nothing has touched, which is the opposite of what an
operator needs while the disk is full. The alert state machine is simply not consulted
for it: the skip is the one completion path that records its event and stops there, which
keeps the fact where it is used instead of on `MaintenanceRun`, a value the status and
trigger APIs project onto the wire. The `gc.store.maintenance.done` event a skipped cycle
emits is long-standing behavior and unchanged here; `StoreDiskCritical` is what tells
operators why the cycle skipped.

Two smaller ones: `Failing since` names the run that opened the outage rather than the
run where the failure last changed shape, because an operator reads that line as the
length of the outage; and the suppressed-repeat count stays per shape, with the line it
prints on saying so.

## Lock discipline

`emitRunEvent` now mutates mu-guarded alert state, so it is renamed
`emitRunEventLocked` to say so, and the three pre-existing test call sites go through
the same locked helper the new tests use. Holding the lock across the alert send is not
new contention: it is the cycle lease, already held for the whole multi-minute
maintenance run.

## Two things in here that are not the feature

`go test -race ./internal/supervisor/` reported a data race on every run **before**
this branch, at `ea361ee1b7`: `maintenanceSmokeTimeout` is a package var that one
`t.Parallel()` test writes while others read it through the probe. Both sides are
parallel, so it surfaces and hides with scheduling, which is how a red `-race` run in
this package came to read as noise. The second commit makes the timeout a per-loop
field defaulting to the same constant, so the test shortens its own loop. No production
behavior changes. It is here because this PR adds parallel tests to that package, and
otherwise its own `-race` gate could not be trusted.

The mail examples in the help text and the CLI reference lose their role names. Help
text feeds the generated docs, so a role name there leaks into published documentation.
The `--dedup` help and the `gc-mail` skill both say that dedup needs a provider which can
query its own history, and that one which cannot sends normally, so suppression does not
read as a guarantee. The skill's archive section said the operation deletes the bead; it
closes it, and the section keeps its warning that there is no way back.

`spawn-storm-detect.sh` is the first caller. It mails once when a bead's reset count
crosses the threshold rather than on every sweep for as long as the storm lasts, and
passes `--dedup` so a ledger reset cannot re-alert while the previous mail is still live.
An edge trigger carries the same hazard as the fingerprint above: the count is saved
whether the mail went out or not, and a count left at the threshold never equals it
again, so a failed send rolls that bead's count back and the next sweep crosses again.

## Test plan

```
gofmt -l cmd/gc internal/mail internal/supervisor
go build ./... && go vet ./...
go test ./internal/mail/... ./internal/supervisor/
go test -race ./internal/mail/... ./internal/supervisor/
go test ./cmd/gc/
go test ./internal/testpolicy/... ./test/docsync/
shellcheck internal/bootstrap/packs/core/assets/scripts/spawn-storm-detect.sh
golangci-lint run ./internal/mail/... ./internal/supervisor/... ./cmd/gc/...
```

All pass at this head. The dedup surface is covered case by case: suppression while a
live copy exists, suppression across two routes to one mailbox, a read-but-unarchived
copy still suppressing, a resend after archive, scoping by key and by recipient
separately, a missing key refused, the CLI suppressing, the CLI reporting it in JSON,
and the CLI falling back when the provider lacks the capability.

The alert state machine is covered transition by transition, including the ones that
only appear when mail is unreliable. Each claim was run against a mutation of the
production code it should catch:

| Mutation | Test that goes red |
| --- | --- |
| dedup compares the raw stored assignee | suppression across two routes to one mailbox |
| the state advances on a failed send | the failure alert retried after a send failure |
| suppression ignores whether the alert was delivered | the same |
| the rotation error wraps the `*LinkError` verbatim | one unchanged condition over three real cycles, rotation case only |
| the fingerprint is the stage alone | repeats suppressed, error changed within one stage |
| `alertSince` is reassigned on every shape change | the recovery notice naming the streak start |
| the skipped-cycle guard is deleted | a disk-critical skip treated as recovery |
| the owed-recovery branch is deleted | a new outage after an undelivered recovery |
| the skipped cycle is routed back through the normal completion path | a disk-critical skip treated as recovery |

The cross-cycle case drives real cycles through the snapshot stage rather than
hand-built run values, with an advancing clock and three separate failure modes, so it
pins both that the error text holds still and that the suppression works on it. The
rotation mode blocks `rename(2)` with an occupied destination rather than a read-only
parent, so it does not depend on file modes a root test runner would ignore.

title: feat(reconciler): claim-side backstop — nudge a seat whose OWN open ready work sits unclaimed (closes the born-wedged-before-claiming gap for named + pool seats)
body:
## Summary

Interactive (turn-based) seats only act when a message is submitted into them — they don't poll their hook. All existing "go claim" signals fire at session boundaries (spawn/wake/sling-time nudge), so a seat that is already awake when its work becomes ready is **never told**: the work sits open/unclaimed indefinitely. Reproduced live twice: a PM seat's `canonicalize-issue` sat unclaimed ~3h (fixed in minutes by one manual pane nudge), and two pool reviewer seats sat 22h on own-assigned work. The recently-merged execution backstop (#6287) covers only `in_progress` claims; `poolClaimBackstop` is pool-gated and keys on `gc.trigger_bead_id`, not the seat's own work. (ga-evxqd — the predicted residual of ga-lez12, reproduced on the pilot rerun.)

## What this adds

A fourth predicate over the existing shared nudge-backstop engine (`cmd/gc/claim_backstop.go`): when a governed seat (pool or configured-named; manual/dependency-only excluded) is awake and quiet past the grace window while its **own** open ready work — routed-to-self or assigned-to-self, zero unmet blocking deps (real deps, not the stale-able `is_blocked` projection), not deferred/held, not its own drain step — sits unclaimed, deliver the default claim nudge on the engine's existing grace→nudge→backoff ladder. **Nudge-only, re-arm (no latch), no drain** — nothing is stranded in_progress, so a drain would be wrong; the lane just keeps re-delivering the missing signal and emits a typed `execution.claim_stalled` for observability.

### Sibling-lane partition (no double-nudging)
1. `in_progress` rows → execution backstop's turf (this lane yields).
2. The seat's bound trigger bead → pool-claim lane's turf.
3. Continuation-shaped rows (`continuation_group` + `session_affinity=require`) → continuation lane's turf **only when the owning seat is pool-managed** (that lane governs only pool seats); on named seats those rows are this lane's to serve — otherwise they'd be covered by neither lane.

### Robustness
- Readiness probes are budgeted (8/tick) with a **persisted rotating window** (coverage tiles the full queue over time; a queue-heavy seat can't be silently un-probed) — rotation paced on the backoff clock, logged only on advance.
- Revalidates each row pre-delivery; fail-toward-HOLD on read errors (never fabricates a nudge, never goes silent-CLEAR on a failure tick).
- Integration-seam test drives real `buildDesiredState` → `beadReconcileTick` (mutation-proven at both seams) so a future re-scope can't silently disable the lane.

## Review notes (minors from the adversarial council, left for reviewer preference)
- A **durable** pool/named alias collision (same assignee identity on both a live pool slot and a live named seat) breaks toward exclusion for the collision window; the in-code "transient ambiguity" comment overstates — could detect mixed ownership and decline to defer.
- `poolManagedSeatIdentities` hand-mirrors the continuation lane's `governs` clause; delegating to `(poolContinuationBackstop{}).governs(s)` would make drift impossible.

## Tests

RED-then-GREEN throughout (16+ lane tests + rotation/pacing/partition/integration): named-seat own-routed-work nudged; continuation row on a pool seat left to the continuation lane; continuation row on a named seat served; rotation reaches a late-sorting ready row and paces its writes; re-arm never latches. Full `./cmd/gc` green.
