title: feat(github-monitor): author allow-list for native pr_monitor (fail-closed)
body:
## Summary

Adds an optional, fail-closed author allow-list to the native `[[github.pr_monitor]]` config plus a matching `gc github pr backfill --author <login>` flag, so an operator can scope the native PR monitor to specific PR authors (e.g. their own) instead of acting on every open PR against a monitored repo/base branch. Implements #6279.

## Changes

- **config** (`internal/config/github_pr_monitor.go`): new `authors` field on `GitHubPRMonitor` (`toml:"authors,omitempty"`), an `AllowedAuthorSet()` helper (trim/dedupe, case-sensitive keys, blank-only collapses to "no restriction"), and validation that rejects an empty author entry.
- **githubmonitor** (`internal/githubmonitor/{monitor,client}.go`): plumb the PR author login end to end — fetch `author { login }` in the GraphQL query, decode it (null actor -> empty), and carry it on `PullRequest` and `Result`. New `EvaluatePullRequestsWithAllowedAuthors(monitor, prs, extraAuthors)` applies the fail-closed filter; the existing `EvaluatePullRequests` delegates to it with no extra authors, so behavior is unchanged when nothing is configured.
- **cmd/gc** (`cmd/gc/cmd_github.go`): repeatable `--author` flag on `backfill`, threaded into evaluation. It unions with each monitor's configured `authors` for that run.
- **docs**: regenerated `docs/reference/config.md`, `docs/reference/cli.md`, and `docs/reference/schema/city-schema.{json,txt}` via `go run ./cmd/genschema` (keeps `check-schema` green).
- **tests**: config (parse `authors`, reject empty entry, `AllowedAuthorSet`), githubmonitor (skip non-matching author, allow match, fail-closed on empty/unresolved author, case-sensitivity, flag∪config union, flag-alone restriction, decode author incl. null actor), and a `cmd/gc` end-to-end test that `--author alice` reports only alice's PR and skips another author's and an unresolved-author PR.

## Fail-closed semantics

- Effective allow-list = configured `authors` ∪ `--author` values.
- **Empty** allow-list -> act on all PRs (historical behavior; backward compatible).
- **Non-empty** allow-list -> act ONLY on PRs whose author login matches an allowed value **exactly and case-sensitively**. A PR whose author is **unresolved/empty** is skipped, never marked actionable, and never mints a repair bead. The default answer for a PR under a configured allow-list is *skip*; a PR becomes eligible only by affirmatively matching.

## Why

The native monitor previously had no author dimension — only repo + base branch — so pointing it at a shared repo made it act on everyone's PRs. This is the root-cause fix for the incident in #6279 (repair beads minted for ~43 PRs the operator did not author; downstream automation then commented/pushed on them).

## Open questions (from the issue, flagged for maintainers)

1. Should a scalar `author` be accepted as sugar for a single-entry `authors`? (Not implemented here.)
2. `--author` currently **unions** with configured `authors`; would you prefer **override** for ad-hoc runs?
3. Case-sensitive exact match (chosen, most auditable) vs case-insensitive login comparison. Easy to switch.

Happy to adjust any of these.

## UAT

```bash
# Build (macOS bakes the ICU rpath):
make build   # or: go build ./cmd/gc

# Config allow-list — add to a city's [[github.pr_monitor]]:
#   authors = ["<your-login>"]
# Then, against a repo with actionable PRs by multiple authors:
gc github pr backfill <monitor-name> --json | jq '.results[].author'
# Expect: only PRs authored by <your-login> appear; others are absent.

# Ad-hoc flag scoping (no config change needed):
gc github pr backfill --author <your-login> --json | jq '.result_count'
# Expect: count reflects only your PRs; PRs with an unresolved author are skipped.

# Unit/behavioral tests:
go test ./internal/config/... ./internal/githubmonitor/...
go test ./cmd/gc -run TestGitHubPRBackfill
```

Note: the `cmd/gc` **test** package currently fails to compile on `main` for an unrelated reason (`pool_session_name_route_assignee_liveness_test.go` calls `releaseOrphanedPoolAssignments` with a stale signature) — not touched by this PR. The `github pr backfill` tests here pass once that pre-existing break is resolved; I verified them locally by building the package with that unrelated file excluded.

Refs #6279

title: feat(github-monitor): author allow-list for native pr_monitor (fail-closed)
body:
## Summary

The native `[[github.pr_monitor]]` monitor — the config consumed by the `gc` supervisor that drives `gc github pr backfill --create-repair-beads` — has **no way to restrict which PR _authors_ it acts on**. It evaluates and mints CI-repair beads for every open PR against a monitored repo/base branch, regardless of who opened it. This proposes an `author`/`authors` allow-list on the monitor config plus a matching `gc github pr backfill --author <login>` flag, with **fail-closed** semantics, so an operator can scope the monitor to their own PRs.

## Background / current behavior

The monitor config exposes only these fields (`internal/config/github_pr_monitor.go`, `GitHubPRMonitor`):

`name`, `owner`, `repo`, `base_branches`, `rig`, `notify`, `repair_route`, `repair_workflow`, `webhook_secret_env`, `webhook_secret_key`, `poll_interval`, `merge_queue`

There is no author field. `gc github pr backfill` (`cmd/gc/cmd_github.go`) exposes only:

`--all`, `--create-repair-beads`, `--json`, `--timeout`

There is no `--author`. The GraphQL query (`internal/githubmonitor/client.go`, `pullRequestsQuery`) doesn't even fetch the PR author, and `githubmonitor.PullRequest` / `Result` carry no author field, so nothing downstream can filter on it. `EvaluatePullRequests` (`internal/githubmonitor/monitor.go`) filters only by base branch before classifying a PR as actionable and (with `--create-repair-beads`) creating a routed repair bead via `ensureGitHubPRRepairBead`.

Net effect: point a monitor at a shared repo and it will act on **everyone's** open PRs.

## Why this matters (real incident)

A monitor pointed at a shared repo minted CI-repair beads for ~43 PRs that were **not** authored by the operator. Downstream repair automation then commented on and pushed to those PRs. The blast radius was other contributors' PRs, and the operator was removed from a GitHub org as a result. There is currently no in-product control that would have prevented this — the only knobs are repo + base branch, both of which were legitimately correct; the missing dimension is **author**.

A downstream mitigation is shipping in the meantime (con-voyage-gascity is adding an author gate in its `ci-repair` workflow plus a bead guard), but that only protects one consumer's workflow. The root cause is that the native monitor has no author scoping, so the fix belongs here in gc-core where the beads are minted.

## Proposed change

**1. Config schema** — add an author allow-list to `[[github.pr_monitor]]`:

```toml
[[github.pr_monitor]]
name          = "my-prs"
owner         = "gastownhall"
repo          = "gascity"
base_branches = ["main"]
rig           = "core"
repair_route  = "..."
authors       = ["kriscoleman"]   # NEW: allow-list of GitHub author logins
```

**2. Backfill flag** — add a repeatable `--author <login>` flag to `gc github pr backfill` that unions with (or, if you prefer, overrides — see open questions) the configured allow-list for that invocation.

**3. Plumbing** — fetch `author { login }` in the GraphQL query, carry it on `githubmonitor.PullRequest` and `Result`, and enforce the allow-list inside `EvaluatePullRequests` (the single choke point every actionable PR and every repair bead already flows through).

## Fail-closed semantics (the important part)

- If the effective allow-list (config `authors` ∪ `--author` values) is **empty**, behavior is unchanged — the monitor acts on all PRs as it does today. This keeps the change backward compatible.
- If the effective allow-list is **non-empty**, the monitor/backfill acts **only** on PRs whose author login **exactly and case-sensitively** matches an allowed value.
  - GitHub logins are case-insensitive for login-in but the API returns canonical casing; requiring an exact match keeps the gate unambiguous and auditable. (If maintainers prefer case-insensitive matching, that's a reasonable alternative — noted in open questions.)
- Any PR whose author is **unresolved or empty** (e.g. deleted/ghost account, or the field came back null) is **skipped**, never treated as actionable, and never gets a repair bead. Absence of proof of authorship is treated as "not allowed," not as "allowed."

The guiding principle: when an allow-list is configured, the default answer for a PR is **skip**, and a PR only becomes eligible by affirmatively matching an allowed login.

## Acceptance criteria (BDD)

```
Given a [[github.pr_monitor]] with authors = ["alice"]
When gc github pr backfill runs against a repo with an actionable PR by "bob"
Then that PR is skipped: no result row when actionable-only, and no repair bead is created

Given a [[github.pr_monitor]] with authors = ["alice"]
When an actionable PR by "alice" is observed
Then it is evaluated and (with --create-repair-beads) a repair bead is created as today

Given a [[github.pr_monitor]] with authors = ["alice"]
And an actionable PR whose author login is empty/unresolved
When backfill runs
Then that PR is skipped (fail-closed), not repaired

Given a [[github.pr_monitor]] with no authors configured
When backfill runs
Then behavior is unchanged (all PRs evaluated) — backward compatible

Given a [[github.pr_monitor]] with authors = ["alice"]
When backfill is invoked with --author bob
Then the effective allow-list is {alice, bob} and PRs by either are eligible
(pending the union-vs-override decision below)
```

## Open questions

1. **Field name**: `authors` (plural list) is proposed. Should a scalar `author` also be accepted as sugar for a single-entry list?
2. **Flag vs config semantics**: should `--author` **union** with the configured allow-list (proposed) or **override** it for that run? Override is arguably safer for ad-hoc "just my PRs right now" use; union is more predictable. Happy to go either way.
3. **Case sensitivity**: exact case-sensitive match (proposed, most auditable) vs case-insensitive login comparison (friendlier). Either is fail-closed; just needs a decision.
4. Should an empty-string entry in `authors` be a config validation error (proposed) rather than silently ignored?

## Scope

Small, self-contained, security-relevant. Touch points: `internal/config/github_pr_monitor.go` (+ validation), `internal/githubmonitor/{monitor,client}.go` (author field + query + fail-closed filter), `cmd/gc/cmd_github.go` (`--author` flag + threading), plus tests in the adjacent `_test.go` files and a `docs/reference/config.md` / schema regen. No changes to bead dedupe or routing.

Filed on behalf of @kriscoleman.

title: feat(beads): proxied-local bd-owned Dolt by default on beads v1.3.0-rc.2
body:
## Supported rc.2 migration path

There is exactly one, and it is a command:

```bash
gc stop                                        # mandatory, not hygiene
gc beads city migrate-proxied [--dry-run] [--json] [--rig NAME]
gc doctor --fix && gc doctor                   # backfill what the old init predates
gc start
```

**Preconditions.** A city initialised the legacy GC-managed way: `metadata.json`
`dolt_mode: server` (or no `dolt_mode` at all), `gc.endpoint_origin: managed_city`, one
gc-owned `dolt sql-server` over `<city>/.beads/dolt`, no `.gc/scope-ownership.json` entry.
gc's server must be **stopped**, and the command proves it rather than trusting it: no
published `dolt-state.json`, no live process holding the data-dir lock, nothing listening on
the port in `.beads/dolt-server.port`. That fence is re-checked at the start of every scope's
turn and again immediately before `bd migrate` — bd's own precondition consults only its own
pid file, cannot see a server gc started, and would commit the mode flip onto a data dir Dolt
still holds locked.

**What it does**, per scope, city first (a rig sharing the city's data dir cannot be proxied
while the city is still direct):

1. `dolt init` the **city's** data dir when `.dolt/repo_state.json` is missing — additive,
   beside the existing database directories — and only when the city's own database is in
   there, or the directory is empty.
2. Give a shared-root rig the **relative** `dolt_data_dir` that roots it at the city's data
   dir. Relative is mandatory: beads drops an absolute value on save and `bd migrate` saves
   partway through the flip.
3. Run bd's own `bd migrate from-server-to-proxied-server --idle-timeout 0`.
4. Verify bd's **outcome** — `metadata.json` says `proxied-server`, the in-flight journal is
   gone — not its exit code.
5. Rewrite `.beads/config.yaml` through gc's canonical writer, which is what drops
   `dolt.mode` and gc's managed endpoint keys.
6. Retire gc's own publication: `<scope>/.beads/dolt-server.port`, and for the city the whole
   `.gc/runtime/packs/dolt` pack state. Nothing else comes back for it.
7. `bd ping` the scope.

**Refusals**, all typed, all by name, none of which mutate anything: already proxied
(`already-migrated`, exit 0), embedded, doltlite (recognised by either metadata field),
external endpoint, journaled in `.gc/scope-ownership.json`, already handed to bd by a
committed ownership journal, a rig with its own store *and* a database in the city's dir, a
rig gc cannot place at all, and a city whose data dir holds databases but not its own.

**Rollback story.** There is no reverse migration on rc.2 and this PR does not invent one.
What it gives instead is that **failure is per scope and resumable**: completed scopes stay
migrated, the failed one is reported with its reason, and rerunning the command finishes the
rest — including a rig whose `dolt_data_dir` was written by the run that then failed at
`bd migrate`. Underneath, bd's own migrate journal is what makes a half-finished flip
recoverable; gc verifies that journal is gone before it calls the scope migrated. Going back
further than that means restoring the city from backup.

`--dry-run` prints the exact per-scope plan (every step above, named) and writes nothing.
`--json` is schema'd at `schemas/beads/city/migrate-proxied/result.schema.json`.
Runbook: **`engdocs/runbooks/beads-migrate-proxied.md`**.

## The journaled ownership handoff is NOT in this PR

An earlier revision of this branch carried a hidden `gc dolt-state handoff-inspect` /
`handoff-stop` protocol: bd would spawn gc as a subprocess and take its typed JSON answers as
proof. **That is withdrawn, because bd never calls gc.** bd spawns nothing but `dolt`; it has
no provider, hook or callback into its caller; everything it needs about the caller arrives as
command-line input. A transfer built the other way makes bd's ownership journal depend on a
binary it cannot verify and makes gc's refusals reachable only through bd.

When the handoff lands it will be **gc-orchestrated over bd verbs** — a phased, journal-driven
`bd migrate ownership-handoff` (`prepare` → `legacy-gone` → `configure` → `verify` → `commit`,
with `rollback`/`rollback-finish` and a non-mutating `status`), with bd owning the journal, the
replacement server, the fences and the rollback, and gc stopping and restarting only its own
legacy server in between. No beads tag has those verbs, so gc ships no driver for one.

What this PR **keeps** is the reading half, which that design still needs: the committed-journal
projection and the three-arm provider-ownership classification, so a scope bd has taken over is
recognised as bd's the moment such a journal exists. On rc.2 nothing writes one, and gc never
will — it is bd's record of bd's own transfer.

Also gone with the protocol: the `gc.json.raw_protocol` cobra annotation, which had no other
user, and the strict managed-stop identity arm, which no non-protocol caller ever passed an
identity to.

## Summary

On beads `v1.3.0-rc.2`, a **fresh** `gc init` with no transport selector now produces a
**bd-owned proxied-local store**: bd runs a `db-proxy-child` supervising a `dolt sql-server`
under `<scope>/.beads/dolt`, and Gas City never starts a Dolt process of its own for that
scope. `gc doctor`, `gc bd`, `gc rig add`, `gc start`, `gc status` and `gc stop` all work
against it, on Linux, proven end to end against the real rc.2 binary.

What changes for a fresh city:

- **bd owns the lifecycle.** `.beads/metadata.json` `dolt_mode: proxied-server` is the
  topology authority. Gas City keeps only `.gc/scope-ownership.json` as a crash-safe
  *intent* journal (`provider_initializing` → `ready`). No second topology store.
- **The proxy is pinned resident.** GC-owned proxied scopes initialise with
  `--proxied-server-idle-timeout 0` (sidecar `idle_timeout: -1`); without it every bd
  command after a quiet period pays a 0.6–6 s proxy + Dolt cold start.
- **Every proxied scope is stopped.** `gc stop`/`shutdown` retires the city's proxy and
  each rig's — each workspace has its own proxy root — and stop is re-runnable.
- **The managed-Dolt verbs stand down.** The dolt pack's orders fire on every city;
  on a bd-owned scope each is a typed no-op (exit 0, `bd-owned-proxied-scope`), and the
  cleanup reaper protects a `dolt sql-server` whose config sits beside a live `proxy.pid`.
- **Escape hatch:** `gc init --beads-transport direct --beads-target local` still gives a
  bd-owned *server*-mode store (`.beads/dolt-server.pid`/`.port`), and `gc stop` retires it.
- **Existing scopes are unchanged.** A persisted `server`, `embedded`, DoltLite or external
  binding keeps its lifecycle; only a scope with no persisted Beads identity takes the
  proxied-local default.

## Design pointers

Epic `ga-p9iuv` (accepted architecture, decisions 1–23). Slice 1 design: decisions D1–D7
plus the red-team revisions R1–R9.

| | |
|---|---|
| D1 | Topology authority is bd. `dolt_mode` in metadata.json; `.gc/scope-ownership.json` is intent only. |
| D2 | Store for proxied scopes is BdStore (the bd CLI front door). rc.2 has **no library open** for a proxied workspace. |
| D3 | Proxy residency is gc's to request, bd's to enforce: idle-never on init, `bd dolt stop` per scope on stop, never `bd dolt start`/`status` on a proxied scope. |
| D4 | Doctor takes the minimal 6004 subset: metadata `dolt_mode` backfill, proxied guards in the beads/rig checks, pending-scope awareness. |
| D5 | ~~Journaled handoff is slice 3, responder side only.~~ **Withdrawn.** bd never calls gc, so there is no responder side; the handoff becomes gc-orchestrated over bd verbs when beads has them. See the section above. |
| D6 | Existing cities migrate through `gc beads city migrate-proxied` — a command, because the residue is gc's to handle. On rc.2 it is the only supported path. |
| D7 | One consolidated PR supersedes #6011 and #6044. |
| R1 | Provider-owned = journal entry **or** persisted proxied binding, so migrated and cloned scopes are covered; a proxied binding with no store is a typed refusal, not a silent empty store. |
| R2 | `BEADS_DOLT_AUTO_START=0` is inert on rc.2's proxied path — any bd read restarts the proxy. Stop retires readers first and the provider's processes last. |
| R3 | The `proxied_provider` gate is expected, not a degradation: doctor reports the bd-owned store OK. |
| R4 | The default pack composition's dolt orders are typed no-ops on a bd-owned scope, and the reaper protects bd's processes — including under test temp roots. |
| R5 | Readiness is a bounded `bd ping`; the owned-proxied op budget is 60 s. |
| R6 | D2 is a measured regression; numbers below, native-over-proxy filed as the follow-up. |
| R7 | go.mod carries `v1.3.0-rc.2` verbatim; `bdFreshProviderMinVersion` is anchored by a test; the resource census and TESTING.md ratchets are recomputed. |
| R8 | A pending external endpoint is journaled, so a retried init does not die for want of it. |
| R9 | No gitignore change — `.gc/` is ignored wholesale. |

## Deliberately not in this PR

- **Native SQL over the proxy.** Every proxied read and write goes through the bd CLI
  (D2) — one process per operation. Measured on this branch through a warm proxy:
  `gc status` **2.06 s**, `gc bd list --json` **2.04 s** (see the timing table below).
  Dialing `127.0.0.1:<proxy.pid port>` is feasible but is a separate design (connection
  lifetime, idle semantics, proxy identity). Filed as a P1 follow-up under `ga-p9iuv`.
- **The journaled legacy→bd ownership handoff.** Not here in any form — see the section
  above. `gc beads city migrate-proxied` is the rc.2 path and is not a placeholder for it.
- **The external-topology remainder of #6004** (TCP/Unix/TLS sidecar support). #6004 stays
  open for it.
- **Dashboard `bd ping`** (#6023) — slice 2. Without it a proxied rig reads down/warn,
  because `bd doctor --readonly` is refused in proxied mode.

Supersedes #6011 and #6044. Neither is closed by this PR. **#6288 is stacked on this branch.**

## Acceptance criterion: every way in, and the way across

The binding criterion added to this slice was *"full coverage of our startup and relevant
integration tests against multiple ways to init, as well as versions that were init the old
way and migrated to the proxied server."* It is met by two things that did not exist before:
a matrix over every supported init shape (**AC-M**), and a real migration of a real old-way
city (**AC-X**). Both run through the real `gc` and `bd` front doors against
`bd v1.3.0-rc.2` and a real `dolt` — no stubs, no hand-edited fixtures standing in for a
lifecycle.

### AC-M — the init topology matrix

`test/acceptance/helpers/beads_topology.go` describes each supported shape — how to init it,
what must end up on disk, which processes must exist and who owns them, what the ownership
journal must say, and what must survive a stop — and
`test/acceptance/beads_topology_matrix_test.go` walks the same command list over all of them:
`gc init` → `gc doctor` → `gc bd create/list/show` → `gc rig add` → `gc start` on the default
pack composition → `gc status` → `gc stop` → `gc start` → `gc stop`.

| shape | what it is | outcome |
|---|---|---|
| **M1** proxied-local | the new default, no selector | PASS |
| **M2** direct-local | `--beads-transport direct --beads-target local` | PASS — was broken (B1, B4) |
| **M3a** direct-external, alias | `--dolt-host/--dolt-port` | PASS — was broken (B5) |
| **M3b** direct-external, selector | `--beads-transport direct --beads-target external` | PASS — was broken (B3, B6) |
| **M4** proxied-external | local bd proxy fronting an external server | PASS — the only shape that needed no fix |
| **M5** legacy GC-managed | the OLD way: gc-owned sql-server, `dolt_mode: server`, `gc.endpoint_origin: managed_city`, no journal | PASS |
| **M6** doltlite / embedded | explicit embedded backend | PASS — was broken (B2); scoped, see limitations |
| **M7** deferred init | `GC_DOLT=skip`, finished by the next `gc start` | PASS |

M5 is initialised by a **real pre-journal `gc` binary** (`GC_ACCEPTANCE_LEGACY_GC_BIN`), not
by writing the old shape by hand: no gc on this branch can produce it, because `gc init`
journals every fresh scope as provider-owned. Where a shape legitimately cannot satisfy a
step, the test asserts the typed outcome rather than skipping.

### AC-X — an old-way city migrated to the proxied server

The command and its contract are described in full at the top of this body. It is a thin,
idempotent, fail-closed orchestrator of bd's own `bd migrate from-server-to-proxied-server`:
bd keeps the journal, the mode flip and the sidecar; gc owns the ordering, the refusals and
the residue bd cannot see. The lock and port probes are excused when a live `bd
db-proxy-child` is proven to own that root — otherwise the command would fence itself out of
its own second step, since after the city migrates bd's proxy holds the lock for every rig
still waiting.

Reading it end to end against AC-X's rule — *any gc-side residue must be handled by a
documented gc command or the lifecycle, never by hand* — found four outcomes that had no
owner, all fixed here with tests:

| | was | is |
|---|---|---|
| a rig whose `bd migrate` failed | unresumable: the rerun looked under the rig's own `.beads/dolt` while the key it had just written pointed at the city's, and refused | the classifier reads the recorded `dolt_data_dir`, so the rerun sees the root the failed run chose |
| a rig gc cannot place | `dolt init` over its directory — bd migrates onto the new empty store, whatever was there is orphaned | refused by name; the one `dolt init` this command performs is the city's |
| a city whose data dir holds other databases and not its own | same init, same silent orphaning | refused by name (an empty dir is still fine — nothing to lose) |
| a doltlite scope naming the engine in `database` rather than `backend` | reached the migratable arm, because its empty `dolt_mode` reads as the pre-`dolt_mode` legacy server | refused by name |

and two ordering/ownership gaps: the stopped fence now guards the whole scope's turn rather
than only the handoff to bd (`dolt init` writes into the same data dir a live server holds
locked), and gc's own pack publication is retired by the command instead of being left for
an operator to delete.

`TestBeadsMigrateLegacyCityToProxied` builds a legacy city **with the legacy binary**, seeds
issues and deps in the city and a rig, asserts the fixture really is the old way, then
migrates and requires: issues, deps and project identity intact; bd-owned proxied with no
gc-managed `sql-server` and no republished `dolt-state.json`; classified provider-owned so
doctor is green; orders no-op; `gc stop` retires every proxy and is re-runnable; restart
works. `TestBeadsMigrateProxiedRefusesLiveLegacyServer` pins the hazard: a live legacy server
must produce a typed refusal naming `gc stop`, with metadata byte-identical.

Runbook: **`engdocs/runbooks/beads-migrate-proxied.md`** — what "legacy GC-managed" looks like
on disk, the copy-paste procedure, the hazard it fences with bd's actual error text, how to
verify, and recovery per failure mode. It states that this is the supported rc.2 path, that
the journaled handoff is unavailable, and that there is no residue to remove by hand.

## Product bugs this found

Eight, all fixed here with focused tests. Running ordinary commands against ordinary shapes
is what found them; none was visible to the single-shape E2E this slice started with.

| # | bug | impact |
|---|---|---|
| **B1** | a bd-owned **direct** store read as a dead store | `--beads-transport direct --beads-target local` — the documented escape hatch — resolved `dolt runtime state unavailable` on every command, and `gc doctor` called both `beads-store` and `dolt-server` **failures** on a healthy city. Resolution now falls back to the record bd writes (`.beads/dolt-server.pid` + `.port`); the pid file is the discriminator, because gc's managed lifecycle mirrors only the port. |
| **B2** | a **doltlite** city acquired a proxy | the fresh-scope canonical `dolt_mode` did not look at the backend, so once the default flipped, a doltlite city came out of `gc init` carrying the binding the ownership classifier reads as bd-owned proxied — and bd raised a `db-proxy-child` plus a Dolt child over a workspace that is supposed to have neither. |
| **B3** | **direct-external silently used a local server** | the adapter passed bd `--server --external` and nothing else, so bd started a local `sql-server` beside the city and wrote a binding naming no upstream. Init then died in its own readiness check, leaving the journal stuck in `provider_initializing` and a Dolt process nobody asked for running. The adapter now supplies `--server-host`/`--server-port` (and `--server-socket`). |
| **B4** | a doctor warning **no bd-owned rig could ever clear** | every healthy rig on a bd-owned store collected a `dolt-backup` warning whose fix hint prescribed a `dolt backup` against a server gc does not own. The guard keyed on the proxied binding; the transport is not what the check is about. |
| **B5** | **`gc rig add` bricked a hosted-Dolt city** | on a city bound to someone else's Dolt server, the rig got a canonical config with `inherited_city` and no `dolt.host`/`dolt.port` — invalid by the contract's own rule — and from then on the **entire city refused to start**. A short-circuit added to preserve a rig's `dolt_mode` returned the mode *instead of* the inherited state; it is now applied *on top of* it. |
| **B6** | **a rig's beads landed on the wrong server** | a rig added to a direct-external city was initialised against *this* machine, because the city's binding lives only in bd's metadata and neither the inheritance decision nor the endpoint projection read it. The operator's beads were split across two servers, silently, until a restart made the extra local server visible. |
| **B7** | `migrate-proxied --json` **did not work at all** | gc's CLI JSON contract refuses any command with no result schema, so the flag returned `json_unsupported` and printed no report. Found by the first real run; the stubs could not see it. Fixed with the result schema and `writeCLIJSONLineOrExit`. |
| **B8** | the migration **fenced itself out of its own second step** | the entry fence refused whenever *anything* held a Dolt lock under the city data dir — but the moment the city migrates, bd's own proxy holds exactly that lock for every database in the dir, including the rigs still queued. The city succeeded and every rig failed with "run gc stop first". The question is *who owns the process*, not whether one exists. |

Plus **D1**, found by the migration spike rather than by a test: `dolt.mode` in `config.yaml`
shadowed `metadata.json` in **three** places — `ResolveDoltConnectionTarget`,
`ResolveAuthoritativeConfigState` (one layer up, which feeds every canonical config write, so
a migrated scope was canonicalised from its pre-migration state) and `EnsureCanonicalConfig`,
which only ever *set* `dolt.mode` and never deleted it, so no writer in the tree could clear
the key. Metadata is now authoritative everywhere, and the writer owns-it-or-drops-it.

## Review: three council rounds

| round | result | disposition |
|---|---|---|
| **1** (`wf_1fdd396a-944`) | 11 confirmed / 3 refuted / 24 raised | all 11 fixed on the branch — stop no longer short-circuits at the first failing scope (C1), the per-bd-command readiness fan-out that made doctor time out on a one-rig city is gone (C2), journal path-drift is per-entry rather than whole-journal (C3), the init help and engdocs match the code (C4), a retiring op visits `rig:`-keyed scopes with an unparseable `city.toml` (C5), and the rest. |
| **2** (`wf_cbae2493-e25`) | 4 confirmed / 6 refuted / 10 raised | all 4 fixed. **R2-1** the reaper's ownership proof required `basename(argv[0]) == "bd"`, but bd execs its child with `os.Executable()`, so a versioned `BD_BIN` pin lost the R4 protection entirely — the verb plus the resolved `--root` is the proof. **R2-2** the projection cache stamped *after* building, so a rewrite landing mid-build was cached as already-observed; the stamp is now taken first. **R2-3** the proxied `dolt-backup` check stayed OK but read as coverage — there is no backup at all on rc.2, and now doctor says so per rig and once per city. **R2-4** `forgetProxiedScopeRuntimeEnv` had no caller; it has two real ones now, both in-process topology changes. |
| **3** (final) | 12 confirmed | all 12 fixed, each with a test that fails on the unfixed code. The table below maps every finding to the commit that closed it. |

The six refutations in round 2 were checked to the code and are recorded with their reasons;
they are not silently dropped.

### Round 3 — the final council, finding by finding

Every fix carries a proving test that fails on the unfixed code; where a finding had a second
half (a budget to raise, a gap to name), that half is implemented too rather than deferred.

| # | sev | finding | commit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **F1** | high | `gc beads city endpoint` and `gc rig set-endpoint` could reach `EnsureCanonicalMetadata`'s deprecated-key strip on a scope bd owns, erasing its upstream binding — before `--dry-run` could say so. Both doors now refuse an owned scope by name, on every canonicalizer, and a city sweep skips a bd-owned inherited rig instead of writing gc keys into its config. | `9ed2252b4` |
| **F2** | high | the acceptance evidence **never ran in any job**: every one of these tests `t.Skip`ped when bd was absent, and no job installed one — a suite that executed nothing reported green. New required job `Beads / topology acceptance`, plus `GC_REQUIRE_ACCEPTANCE_TOOLING=1` turning a missing bd or dolt into a hard failure. | `55a5e29f9`, `39692ea76`, `bf023549b` |
| **F3** | med | renaming a rig in place made `gc start` refuse the whole city: the journal re-keyed only a detached `path:` record. It now re-keys a `rig:<other>` record whose path matches a configured rig, and the validator only calls a rig-keyed entry drift when its path is no configured rig's. | `52c70d728` |
| **F4** | med | a failing scope sent `recover:` over **every** owned scope in the city. The lifecycle op now returns the failing scope roots, and recovery re-checks only those; health still fans out over the whole city. | `fdd73bfbc` |
| **F5** | med | an interrupted `bd migrate` was reported as `already-migrated` and left there — bd flips `dolt_mode` in metadata.json *before* the journal is retired, so the resumable state reads as the finished one. Verified empirically against the pinned rc.2 bd with `BEADS_MIGRATION_FAIL_PHASE`. The `AlreadyProxied` arm now detects the journal, reruns `bd migrate`, re-verifies, and reports `migrated`. | `b5466e97c` |
| **F6** | med | a standalone bd server was adopted as a *verified* target inside a gc-canonical `managed_city`. ## Known limitations

Each is pinned in the matrix fixture with a comment so it is visible rather than suppressed,
and the allowances are name-scoped and — for warnings — message-scoped.

1. **`identity_match` on bd-owned direct scopes (M2, M3b).** gc's preflight confirms identity
   with a direct SQL probe for `metadata._project_id`, a row rc.2's `bd init --server` does
   not write, so the scope stays on the bd CLI front door with a `BdStore fallback` warning.
   That is where every proxied scope lives *by design* (D2), but the direct transports have
   no equivalent "expected, not degraded" gate. Closing it means deciding whether a bd-owned
   direct scope should be native-open eligible — a design question.
2. **`custom-types:city` on an upgraded city (M5).** A city initialised by an older gc keeps
   that gc's bead vocabulary until an operator runs `gc doctor --fix`; `gc start`
   re-canonicalises `config.yaml` but never writes the store's `custom_types` table. This is
   the upgrade path as it stands and the gap most worth closing next.
3. **M6 is scoped.** doltlite through `GC_BEADS_BACKEND` runs init, a typed front-door
   refusal, and stop. `gc init` never runs the adapter's doltlite init op, so no embedded
   store is created, and it starts a gc-managed `sql-server` that `gc stop` never retires
   because the city is not classified as owning a managed-Dolt lifecycle. **Both are true on
   main**, measured against the pre-journal binary. The matrix records the leak (and kills
   the process so the shape cannot poison the next one) and does not run `gc start` on a
   storeless city.
4. **`RigDoltServerCheck` names the wrong topology for a bd-owned rig.** It classifies by
   whether `config.yaml` carries an explicit endpoint, which a bd-owned rig's never does, so
   it reports the inherited-city skip and never dials the server the rig resolves to. Status
   is OK and `RigBeadsCheck` does dial, so nothing is unhealthy — but it would keep saying OK
   with the wrong topology name even if the rig's own server were dead. Asserted as current
   behaviour, marked.
5. **No backup on the proxied path.** rc.2 lists `backup*` in its proxied refusal matrix, so
   neither gc nor bd can register a recovery point for a proxied scope, and `mol-dog-backup`
   talks to a managed server that does not exist there. The per-scope checks correctly go
   quiet; doctor now states the gap per rig and once per city
   (`proxied-backup-coverage`, advisory). Until beads lifts the refusal the store under the
   proxy root is the only copy.
6. **Option B for migrated rigs is not built.** A migrated rig shares the city's proxy root
   (relative `dolt_data_dir`), which preserves the old process count but is not the shape a
   fresh proxied-local `gc rig add` produces. `bd dolt stop` on such a rig stops the city's
   proxy too, so stop fan-out dedupes by resolved root path. rc.2 has no verb to relocate a
   database between proxy roots, which is what blocks Option B.
7. ~~**Migration residue is documented, not swept.**~~ **Fixed.** "Safe to delete by hand" is
   the one answer AC-X does not allow, and nothing else was coming back for it:
   `clearManagedDoltRuntimeStateUnlessBound` returns early for a scope with a complete bd
   binding, which is exactly what the migration creates. The command retires the whole
   `.gc/runtime/packs/dolt` publication and every scope's `.beads/dolt-server.port` mirror,
   on the migrating run and on any rerun over an already-migrated city.
   `.beads/dolt.gate.lock` still survives, and should: it is bd's file, under bd's directory.
8. **`gc doctor --fix` is part of the documented migration procedure**, not part of the
   command — the missing custom type is limitation 2, an old-init-on-new-gc gap.
9. **rc.3 bd defects worth filing**, all re-confirmed by the real runs: `bd migrate
   --dry-run` returns before its Dolt-root validation, so a dry run "passes" for a state the
   real run refuses; migrate's running-server check consults only bd's own pid file; and
   there is no verb to relocate a database between proxy roots.
10. **Cost.** The matrix is about three hours sequentially, dominated by M2 and M3b, because
    on a bd-owned store every bead read costs a fork. It runs on demand
    (`make test-beads-topology-matrix`), not in the default tier; `ACCEPTANCE_GO_TEST_FLAGS`
    is the sharding seam if it is ever wanted in an RC gate.
11. **Follow-up — gc can migrate a shared external database out from under a co-resident bd.**
    Surfaced while triaging the harness skew above, and worth a bead on its own merits. beads
    #5920's guard is supposed to stop gc auto-applying a pending schema migration to a *shared
    server* database, because doing so locks out every bd client still on the old schema. Observed
    behaviour is that it sometimes refuses (the honest `gate=native_open` fallback) and sometimes
    does not, on the same tree and the same shape — after which the co-resident bd fails with
    `table "leases" does not have column "granted_node"`. The nondeterminism is the defect: a guard
    against an irreversible, multi-client-visible action should not be order-dependent. Not fixed
    here — it is beads-side or at the gc/beads boundary, and it is out of this slice's scope.

native path and the bd CLI: either gc refuses to migrate a shared server database it is ahead of

that reads like a gc defect, or gc migrates it anyway and the co-resident bd is locked out of its
own database (`table "leases" does not have column "granted_node"`), which reads like a beads
defect. Which one you got depended on who reached the database first, so it also looked
nondeterministic.

Both binaries report `1.3.0-rc.2` — they were built from the same tag out of different checkouts —
so no version string could have caught it. With a `bd` rebuilt from the pinned module both shapes
pass, and the numbers above are from that run.

both directions — a bd ahead of the library writes a schema gc's native open cannot read. The guard
only runs when a real bd is configured, so the cells that cannot hit the skew pay nothing.

title: Formula step release is dependency-only: a step that closes with gc.outcome=fail still releases its dependents (failed self-review released the push step)
body:
## What happened

gc 1.4.1, `mol-polecat-commit`. The "Self-review and run tests" step ended with the test suite failing and the agent closed it with `gc.outcome=fail`. The formula then released "Commit to base branch, push, and exit" anyway. The step DAG orders steps by dependency and never by the outcome of the step being depended on, so a failed review step unblocks the push step exactly as a passed one does.

The only reason a known-failing commit did not reach the branch is that the agent declined an action it was authorised to take: it refused to push, closed the push step as fail, and let the workflow close as fail. That happened four more times today across three agents (a self-review claimed with an invalid baseline, then the push step released after it). A review gate whose failure does not gate is not a gate, and with the formula default `base_branch = main` the released push lands on main.

## Where the limitation is

- `internal/formula/types.go` around lines 283 to 286: `Step.Condition` is documented as variable-only (`{{var}}`, `!{{var}}`, `{{var}} == value`, `{{var}} != value`) and is "Evaluated at cook/pour time via FilterStepsByCondition".
- `internal/formula/stepcondition.go` lines 31 to 78: `EvaluateStepCondition` reads only `vars`; nothing at release time can consult a prior step's `gc.outcome`.

So a formula author has no way to express "run this step only if the step it depends on passed". Conditions are decided when the workflow is cooked, before any step has an outcome.

## Suggestions, any one of which would close the gap

1. Fail closed by default: when a step closes with `gc.outcome=fail`, do not release its dependents; close them (or leave them blocked) and let the workflow finalize as failed. A formula that wants the current behaviour could opt in per step (`release_on_fail = true`).
2. Outcome-aware conditions evaluated at release time, for example `condition = "{{steps.review.outcome}} == pass"`, so a formula can branch on a prior step's result (a failure route, a retry step, a notify-only step).
3. A `requires_outcome = "pass"` field on the dependency edge, checked at release time, as a smaller change than a general expression.

Until one of these exists we are adding a fail-closed precondition script at the top of our push step that reads the review step's outcome and exits non-zero if it is not `pass`. That works, but it is a check that every formula author has to remember, and it fails silently at the formula nobody remembers to add it to.

title: feat(graph-v2): expose durable attested review-result receipts
body:
## Problem

A Graph V2 workflow can route a reviewer step, stamp its claiming session, run a controller-owned check, retain per-attempt artifacts, and propagate `gc.output_json` to the logical control. It cannot durably prove which provider/model the reviewer actually used or bind that observation to the reviewed artifact.

This matters when a workflow policy requires one independent reviewer selected dynamically from a qualified model set. The requested `opt_model` and worker-authored `gc.output_json` are claims, not orchestrator-owned evidence of the observed model.

## Reproduction

1. Define a Formula V2 step with `check`, routed to a model-backed reviewer.
2. Let the physical attempt write a structured verdict and `gc.output_json`.
3. Inspect the attempt, logical Ralph control, session record, and artifact directory.
4. The attempt has `gc.session_id` and `gc.session_name`, and the logical control receives output, but there is no durable engine-owned observed provider/model field or digest binding the session observation, verdict, and artifacts.
5. The live session API may expose a model through `Peek`, but that is transient runtime metadata and cannot be replayed as release evidence after the session ends.

Relevant implementation points:

- `cmd/gc/cmd_hook_claim.go` stamps claim/session provenance.
- `internal/dispatch/ralph.go` builds the controller check environment.
- `internal/molecule/artifact.go` defines per-attempt artifact storage.
- `internal/dispatch/control.go` and retry handling propagate `gc.output_json`.
- `internal/bootstrap/packs/core/formulas/mol-review-quorum.toml` provides a worker-authored review scaffold; its Go finalizer is not wired into formula execution.

## Requested capability

Have Gas City stamp a versioned review-result receipt, or provide an equivalent stable accessor, when a checked reviewer step completes successfully. A useful minimum envelope is:

```json
{
  "schema": "gc.review-result.v1",
  "source_bead_id": "...",
  "workflow_root_id": "...",
  "step_id": "...",
  "attempt_bead_id": "...",
  "session_id": "...",
  "provider": "...",
  "observed_model": "...",
  "verdict": "pass|changes_required|fail",
  "output_sha256": "...",
  "artifact_sha256": "..."
}
```

The receipt should be orchestrator-owned, survive session teardown and workflow replay, and be directly consumable by downstream checks without reconstructing `gc.logical_bead_id`, `gc.iteration`, or `gc.step_ref` relationships.

## Acceptance criteria

- A downstream checked step can retrieve the receipt through a documented stable interface.
- Requested and observed models remain distinguishable.
- The receipt binds the physical attempt, claiming session, output, and artifact bytes.
- Missing, ambiguous, or mismatched provenance fails closed.
- A single-review workflow can express `prepare -> checked review -> merge` without graph-topology traversal.

Related but distinct: #5838, #2947, #2843, and #4247.

title: bug(cli): expose convoy status cache age in JSON
body:
## Summary

`gc convoy status --json` drops the cache age returned by the supervisor API. Consumers cannot tell that the convoy/member state is a cached snapshot, even though the human output reports the age.

## Symptom

In a supervisor-managed city, `gc convoy status <id>` may read the API server's cached snapshot while `gc bd show <member>` reads the direct store. The human convoy status output includes a stale-read banner when the snapshot is old, but the JSON result has no equivalent signal.

## Reproduction

Run the API-path renderer with a response carrying `X-GC-Cache-Age-S: 45`:

```text
go test ./cmd/gc -run '^TestRouteConvoyStatusJSONIncludesCacheAge$'
```

The minimal regression fixture returns a valid convoy response and the cache-age header.

Result: expected the JSON object to contain `"_cache_age_s":45` → got a valid convoy object with no `_cache_age_s` key.

## Root cause

`cmd/gc/cmd_convoy.go:1219-1227` renders the API response through `writeConvoyStatusJSON` but passes only the convoy body and progress. `convoyStatusResultJSON` at `cmd/gc/cmd_convoy.go:979-984` has no cache-age field, and the writer at `cmd/gc/cmd_convoy.go:1351-1375` cannot emit one. The API client already returns the header as `CachedRead.AgeSeconds` from `internal/api/client.go:974-994`; the human branch of the same renderer consumes it at `cmd/gc/cmd_convoy.go:1264-1265`.

The violated invariant is that API-backed JSON read surfaces expose the cache freshness signal while direct-store fallback JSON omits it. Without the signal, a consumer can mistake cached state for a direct read.

## Fix candidates

**A. Add the field at the convoy status writer boundary** — add `CacheAgeS *float64` with `json:"_cache_age_s,omitempty"`, pass `&cr.AgeSeconds` from the API renderer, and pass `nil` from the direct-store fallback.
- Scope: 2 files and a focused unit test.
- Trade-off: smallest compatible fix; convoy status gets the same envelope convention as sibling API-backed JSON readers.

**B. Introduce a shared CLI JSON freshness envelope** — move cache-age emission into a common response wrapper used by every API-backed read command, including convoy status.
- Scope: several CLI renderers and their tests.
- Trade-off: more consistent long-term abstraction, but larger compatibility and review surface for a one-field omission.

**Recommendation:** A, because the API client and sibling CLI readers already establish the field convention and the direct fallback must remain unchanged.

## Adjacent / out of scope

This does not change cache semantics, add a cache-bypass flag, or make convoy status a live read. The original convoy-vs-`bd show` disagreement was caused by our operator comparing a cached API view with a direct store view without checking the cache route/age; that report-path misuse is separate from this missing JSON diagnostic.

title: providergov: a single OverflowProviders pool makes claude-required cascade cross-vendor — per-tier overflow policy
body:
## Problem

`Policy.OverflowProviders` is a **single pool shared by both tiers**, and the doc comment states the coupling plainly (`internal/providergov/decision.go:86-88`, read at `fc56f0e`):

```go
// OverflowProviders is the overflow vendor pool in priority order.
// Serves overflow-ok work always and claude-required work on cascade.
OverflowProviders []string
```

`claude-required` reaches that pool at **two** sites, not one:

- `decision.go:180-182` — every Claude account dark ⇒ `Decision{Provider: OverflowProviders[0], Reason: ReasonCascade}`;
- `decision.go:203-205` — already cascading and the re-entry gate refuses (headroom or cooldown) ⇒ the same cascade again.

So the moment an overflow pool is configured for `overflow-ok`, `claude-required` inherits it. The only way to stop regulated work cascading cross-vendor is to leave `OverflowProviders` empty **globally** — which also removes `overflow-ok`'s cushion, the reason the pool exists. It is all-or-nothing, and the safe half of the choice costs you the other half.

Verified live (2026-07-10, Voxist city): `gc provider quota --overflow zai,openrouter` →

```
overflow-ok      zai (overflow)
claude-required  zai (cascade)
```

## Why this matters

The two tiers exist precisely to separate work that may move vendors from work that may not. In our deployment `claude-required` covers MDR Class I (medical dictation), MDR-adjacent, and PII-bearing API paths; the overflow vendors (`api.z.ai`, `openrouter`) are non-EU and non-Claude. A quota cascade that silently re-routes those prompts is a data-residency and model-provenance violation, decided by a *capacity* heuristic that has no idea what it is carrying.

Because the tier annotation is the thing that already encodes "this work may not move", the enforcement belongs in the decision function, not in every consumer.

## Ask

Make the overflow pool **per tier**:

```go
// OverflowByTier is the overflow vendor pool per tier, in priority order.
// A tier absent from the map has no overflow pool: it never cascades.
OverflowByTier map[string][]string
```

- `overflow-ok` — keeps a cross-vendor pool (`zai`, `openrouter`, …). Cascading it is acceptable by definition.
- `claude-required` — its **own** pool, **default empty** ⇒ Claude-only. On all-Claude-dark it should fail open to the Claude primary with a loud event (see the companion fail-open issue) rather than cascade.
- Keep `OverflowProviders` as the `overflow-ok` default so existing configs are unchanged; a deployment that wants today's behaviour sets `claude-required` explicitly, which makes the cross-vendor choice **visible in config** instead of implicit in a shared field.
- The fix must cover **both** cascade sites — `:180-182` and the re-entry-refused branch at `:203-205`.

The default is the point: a deployment gets the EU-sovereign/Claude-only behaviour for regulated work without knowing this issue exists, and opts out deliberately.

## Workaround, and why it is not sufficient

Our reconciler refuses to write a non-Claude provider for a `claude-required`-class tier regardless of what the governor decided — defense in depth for the spawn path only. Any other consumer of `SelectProviderFor` still gets the unsafe cascade, and the guard has to duplicate a tier taxonomy the governor already owns.

## Acceptance

With `OverflowByTier{"overflow-ok": ["zai"], "claude-required": []}` and every Claude account dark:

- `overflow-ok` → `zai`, `Reason = ReasonOverflow`/`ReasonCascade` as today;
- `claude-required` → never a non-Claude provider, on the cascade branch **and** on the re-entry-refused branch; fails open to the Claude primary with an event.
- Existing configs setting only `OverflowProviders` keep today's `overflow-ok` behaviour.

Filed from the Voxist city (downstream beads `vc-u9j`, `vc-22b`; decision record ADR-0021 D-3). Source anchors re-verified against `fc56f0e` (2026-09-07).

title: RFC: city-qualified mail addressing over a shared messaging store ([mail.crosscity])
body:
## Summary

Several independently operated cities share one physical store for the `messaging` bead class — a relocated `[storage.classes.messaging]` binding, the front door #4017 made first-class. In that topology a cross-city mail is a plain read on the receiving side; the only missing piece is an address form that says *which* city a name belongs to.

Proposal: `<city>/<address>`, split on the first `/`, roster-checked against a `[mail.crosscity].cities` list, opaque past the city segment. Senders on cross-city mail are stored city-qualified, so a plain `gc mail reply` on the receiving side routes back across cities with no context switch. `<local city>/<addr>` and `<addr>` are one mailbox. Absent the section, nothing changes.

## Why an RFC rather than a review

It proposes a topology upstream has no reference deployment for. A complete, flag-gated, inert-when-off implementation exists — #5797, held as a draft: ~1,600 lines across `cmd/gc`, `internal/api`, `internal/config`, `internal/mail`, with the resolver core a pure dependency-free type — which is exactly why a yes-or-no on the shape should come before anyone spends review cycles on it. Converted from the draft to an issue per the contributor conventions.

## Relation to existing direction

- `gc context` and #5386 route mail to a *remote* city over the control plane (kubectx for cities). This is complementary, not competing: one address space over a shared store, no wake hop, exactly-once by construction (one bead is the message). We carry #5386's routing on our fork and would like to see it land first. If maintainers would rather cross-city mail always travel the control plane, this RFC should be a no, and we carry nothing — the flag-gated shape means the fork does not depend on it.
- Sender trust, stated plainly: `--from` with a foreign city segment is accepted verbatim. A shared messaging store already means every writer is trusted, exactly as it does for any bead today; the proposal moves that boundary in neither direction. Sender attestation, if wanted, belongs in the store or transport layer, not in address parsing.
- `--notify` on a cross-city recipient is a typed refusal before any write: no cross-machine wake primitive exists, and a nudge queued into a leg that is not there must not report success.

## The ask

1. Appetite yes/no on the shared-messaging-store topology as something upstream is willing to support.
2. Yes/no on the address form (`<city>/<address>` with a config roster), or a preference for sourcing the roster from data.

On a yes, #5797 reopens for line review, split however maintainers prefer (resolver core, CLI wiring, API wiring). On a no, it stays closed and nothing is carried.

## Reference deployment

Three cities over one hub store. A `docs/guides` walkthrough with the real configuration is available if there is appetite.

title: fix(doctor): surface effective city suspension as a doctor check (#6126)
body:
## What

`gc doctor` gave no indication a city was suspended — an operator could run it, see every controller/database check pass, and never learn the reason the city is doing no work is that it's intentionally paused. `gc status --json` already reports this via `suspensionstate.EffectiveCitySuspended`; doctor had no equivalent.

Fixes #6126.

## Fix

New `CitySuspensionCheck` (`internal/doctor/checks_city_suspension.go`), registered in `cmd/gc/cmd_doctor.go` next to `NewLegacySuspendedFieldCheck`:

- Resolves suspension the same way the runtime does (`suspensionstate.EffectiveCitySuspended` merged with `cfg.Workspace.EffectiveSuspendedOnStart`) — no reimplemented logic.
- Distinguishes an explicit `gc suspend` runtime override from the configured `suspended_on_start` default in `city.toml`, with a message naming the right lever for each.
- Reports an unreadable/corrupt `suspension-state.json` as **unknown**, never silently inferred as "not suspended" (a missing file, per `suspensionstate.Load`'s own contract, is not an error and correctly resolves through the normal path).
- `StatusWarning` / `SeverityAdvisory` — informational only, never blocks/gates `gc doctor`'s exit code.
- `CanFix()` always `false` — never offers to auto-resume; suspension is an operator decision.
- Updates the `cmd/gc/testdata/doctor_check_names.golden` fixture to include the new check name.

## Testing

`go build -tags gms_pure_go ./...` clean, `gofmt -l .` empty on all touched files. New `TestCitySuspensionCheck_*` suite (9 tests, covering not-suspended / both suspension sources / unreadable state / no config / nil context / not-fixable / warmup-eligible) all pass, full `internal/doctor` package passes, `TestBuildDoctorChecks_NameSetUnchanged` (golden-fixture registration test) passes.

title: feat: sessions: widen session.wake_refused to name every pre-start wake guard (only held/quarantined/idle-sleep emit today)
body:
## Summary

`session.wake_refused` (#5842, closing #5739) names three refusal guards — `held`, `quarantined`, `idle-sleep` — and the emission is gated on exactly those three strings. At least seven other guards can drop a durable `wake_request=explicit` before any start attempt, and each of them is silent on both channels the event exists to serve: no event, and `wake_attempts` left at 0 (the bump lives inside the emitter). The shape #5739 clause 2 was written to make falsifiable is therefore still unfalsifiable for most of its domain — and it is the shape #5785 is open about.

This is a coverage gap on a payload that shipped six days ago, not a defect in it: the three shipped reasons are correct as far as they go.

## Symptom

A session holds `wake_request=explicit`, is not alive, and never gets a start attempt. Nothing is observable:

```bash
gc events --type session.wake_refused --since 1h                                   # empty
gc bd show <session-bead> --json | jq -c '.metadata | {wake_request, wake_attempts}'  # {"wake_request":"explicit","wake_attempts":0}
```

`gc session wake` has already printed `wake requested.`, so the CLI is success-shaped (#5785 defect 1). Recovery is bead-metadata forensics.

## Reproduction

Two of the unnamed guards, both reachable without a race:

**1. Config sleep suppression (`config_wake_suppressed`).**
- Non-interactive session, no assigned work, `wake_request=explicit`, whose workspace `session_sleep` policy suppresses wake.
- `configWakeSuppressedInfo` returns true and `wakeDemandOverridesSleepSuppression` is false, so the reconciler sets `eval.ConfigSuppressed = true` and clears `eval.Reasons` (`cmd/gc/session_reconciler.go:3634-3637`), then drops the loop-local decision at `cmd/gc/session_reconciler.go:3672-3674` (`if shouldWake && eval.ConfigSuppressed { shouldWake = false }`).
- The emission at `cmd/gc/session_reconciler.go:3720-3728` reads the **raw** `decision.Reason`, which in this path is the demand-set wake reason, not one of the three literals → no event. The comment at `:3712-3719` states this raw-read is deliberate ("a policy override never masks or fabricates a refusal") — and the correct half of that is that a suppression should be *named* rather than fabricated as one of the three.

**2. Not in the desired set (`not_desired`).**
- Any session with `wake_request=explicit` that the awake set does not select. `ComputeAwakeSet` builds `AwakeDecision{HasAssignedWork: …}` and only ever assigns `Reason` inside the branches (`cmd/gc/compute_awake_set.go:429/436/442/448/462/472/515/522/528`); a bead that matches none of them leaves `ShouldWake=false, Reason=""` → the `switch` at `cmd/gc/session_reconciler.go:3721` matches nothing → no event, no counter.

The remaining guards sit after `shouldWake` and before the start, so they never reach the emitter's `!decision.ShouldWake` gate at all: failed-create `continue` (`cmd/gc/session_reconciler.go:3731-3737`), quarantine `continue` (`:3739-3740`), startup-health episode quarantine (`:3742-3762`), start-in-flight `continue` (`:3765-3772`), respawn circuit breaker open (`:3778-3791`), provider-health red (check at `:3799`, red skip `continue` at `:3805-3814`). Those six do record a trace decision (`TraceOutcomeFailedCreate` / `TraceOutcomeStartInFlight` at `cmd/gc/session_reconciler_trace_types.go:257-258`, and siblings such as `TraceReasonProviderRed`/`TraceOutcomeRespawnSkipped` at `:3810`), so the vocabulary already exists in the trace codes — it just does not reach the durable event log or the counter.

## Root cause

The reason vocabulary is a string whitelist in a `switch`, one statement away from the emitter, rather than a property of the decision machinery that produces the refusal:

- `cmd/gc/session_reconciler.go:3720-3728` — `switch decision.Reason { case "held", "quarantined", "idle-sleep": emit… }`, with no default arm.
- `internal/api/event_payloads.go:602-611` — `SessionWakeRefusedPayload` documents `Reason … "held, quarantined, or idle-sleep"` and carries `session_id / session_name / template / reason / wake_request / attempts`. There is no field for a secondary cause, and no `wake_requested_at`, so a consumer cannot tell which config suppressed the wake, until when, or how old the unserved request is.
- `internal/events/events.go:140-148` — the const's own doc comment repeats the three-reason scope, so the narrow vocabulary is now codified in three places.
- `cmd/gc/session_reconciler.go:4832-4852` — `wake_attempts` is incremented *only* inside `emitSessionWakeRefused`, via a direct marker write (deliberately not the accrual path, so a persistent refusal cannot self-quarantine). Consequence: guards outside the whitelist leave `wake_attempts=0` forever, which is precisely the "counter never moves" half of #5739 clause 2.

No `engdocs/design/*.md` covers the wake-refusal vocabulary (`git grep -l 'wake_refused\|wake_request' engdocs/design` → empty), so nothing here contradicts an accepted design. ADR-0013 A1 M3a is referenced in the provider-health gate comment (`cmd/gc/session_reconciler.go:3795-3797`) and is about *skipping respawn*, not about staying silent, so naming that skip is additive.

## Fix candidates

**A. Widen the existing event in place** — replace the three-literal `switch` with a default-emits arm carrying the raw reason (`unknown` when empty / `config_wake_suppressed` when suppressed), and lift the six post-decision `continue` sites to the same emitter, reusing the `TraceOutcomeCode` strings so the two vocabularies are one vocabulary. Extend the payload with `detail` (secondary cause: which policy, `quarantined_until`, breaker identity, provider name) and `wake_requested_at` (the unserved request's age, and a natural throttle key so one request emits once however many ticks refuse it).
- Scope: `cmd/gc/session_reconciler.go` (the gate + ~6 call sites), `internal/api/event_payloads.go`, `internal/events/events.go` doc, then the generated surface (`internal/api/openapi.json`, `docs/reference/schema/openapi.{json,txt}`, `internal/api/genclient/client_gen.go`) — regenerate, never hand-carry. ~±120 lines plus the reconciler tests.
- Trade-off: the `reason` enum grows in the wild, so any consumer that switched on the three literals must handle new values (all `omitempty` additions are backwards-compatible; only `reason`'s domain widens). Emits from the six post-decision gates need the same throttle guard or a red provider will write an event per session per tick.

**B. Make the vocabulary structural** — introduce a typed `WakeGuard` enum in `internal/session` that the awake set, the reconciler gates and the payload all draw from, so adding a guard that can refuse a wake without naming it does not compile. The event then emits for every refusal by construction and `wake_attempts` is bumped at the single decision point rather than inside the emitter.
- Scope: `internal/session` (new type + the awake-set sites), `cmd/gc/compute_awake_set.go`, `cmd/gc/session_reconciler.go`, `internal/api/event_payloads.go`, generated surface. Roughly 2-3× candidate A, and it moves `wake_attempts` accounting off the emitter — which is its own behaviour change and needs the #5739 throttle tests restated.
- Trade-off: closes the class permanently (the next guard added cannot be unnamed, which is how this gap was missed once already) at the cost of touching the awake-set contract that #5802 and the residency work also edit.

**Recommendation: A now, B as a follow-up question.** A turns the event from a 3-of-11 sample into a complete one (the three awake-set reasons it names, against the eleven distinct refusal paths above) without disturbing the awake-set contract, and its payload fields are what a patrol consumer needs to act on #5785. Whether the vocabulary should be a typed enum (B) is an architectural call worth making before a third reader hardcodes the strings. Maintainer's call.

## Adjacent / out of scope

- **Not bundled with the `suspended_at` coherence half** of the same finding: different file, different owner decision, tracked on #5739 (see the re-check comment there). This issue asks only for refusal naming.
- The `wake_refused_event_at` throttle is cleared only by `ClearWakeBlockersPatch` (`internal/session/lifecycle_transition.go:245`) — not by `PreWakePatch` (`:203-221`, which clears `wake_request`/`wake_requested_at` themselves) — and `ClearWakeBlockersPatch`'s only production caller (`cmd/gc/session_beads.go:508-509`) `delete`s the `state` key before applying it — so on a session where the marker is set once, later distinct refusals may be throttled out entirely. Whichever candidate lands, the throttle identity deserves a look: keying on the *request* (`wake_requested_at`, cleared by `PreWakePatch` when a wake is served) rather than on "an event was ever emitted" makes "one request, one event" true without making "one bead, one event forever" true by accident.
- #3975 (silent wake no-op when there are no wake reasons) is the same failure shape at a different guard; this issue would give #3975 a name to print, but does not subsume it.
- Generated surface must be regenerated after any rebase rather than cherry-picked — `internal/api/openapi.json` / `docs/reference/schema/*` / `internal/api/genclient/client_gen.go` resolve blob conflicts silently wrong, which is what makes this family expensive to re-port locally.

title: Let an agent select its runtime, so infrastructure agents need not share the city's GUI backend
body:
## The problem

A city's runtime backend is chosen city-wide, so infrastructure agents and work
agents must share one. They want different ones, and forcing them together is
what makes a GUI-backed runtime unusable for a long-lived city.

Concretely: driving Daintree through an exec provider, a `mayor` and a `bd.dog`
pool have to live in Daintree panels, because the rig agents do. But Daintree
keeps project views in an LRU capped at five, and an external client bound to a
workspace cannot act once that view is evicted
(daintreehq/daintree#12316). So the city's own agents — which nobody ever
watches — are hostage to whether the operator happens to have the city's own
project among their five most recent.

The result is thousands of failed starts and a mayor that either cannot start or
runs where it cannot be managed. Not Daintree's fault: a mayor does not need a
GUI panel, and putting it in a view cache is the wrong home for it.

## The machinery already exists

`resolveSessionTransportProvider` already builds a per-session router and sends
named sessions to a second provider:

```go
autoSP := sessionauto.New(base, acpSP)
for _, sessName := range acpRouteNames {
    autoSP.RouteACP(sessName)
}
```

It is hardcoded to ACP. The per-agent `session` field looks like the seam for
this but is a *transport* selector accepting only `acp`, `tmux` or omission
(`IsValidSessionTransport`), so `session = "tmux"` under a non-tmux city is
neither honored nor rejected — the agent silently falls back to the city
default.

## The ask

Let an agent select the **runtime**, not just the transport, using the router
that is already there. Something like:

```toml
[[agents]]
name = "mayor"
runtime = "tmux"          # infrastructure: headless, always reachable

[[agents]]
name = "core.control-dispatcher"
# unset: inherits the city default, e.g. exec:gc-session-daintree
```

Rules that seem right from outside, but you know the model:

- Unset inherits the city default, so nothing changes for existing cities.
- An unknown or unbuildable runtime fails at config validation, not at launch.
- It composes with the ACP routing rather than replacing it.

## Why this is the right split

The two kinds of agent genuinely differ:

| | infrastructure (`mayor`, `bd.dog`) | work agents (rig dispatchers) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| watched by a human? | never | yes, that is the point |
| needs a GUI panel? | no | yes |
| lifetime | as long as the city | as long as the task |
| where it should live | headless (tmux) | the IDE, in the repo being worked on |

Split that way, both problems disappear. The mayor runs in tmux — no view, no
eviction, no storms, reachable forever. Rig agents run in the IDE, in the
project the operator has open, which is exactly when that project's view is
resident. Each backend gets the work it is actually good at.

Without it, the choice is all-or-nothing: put everything in the IDE and accept
that the city stops when the operator navigates away, or put everything in tmux
and lose the IDE integration entirely. Both are worse than the mix, and the mix
is one config field away from machinery that already ships.

## Environment

gc 1.4.1, `[session] provider = "exec:gc-session-daintree"`, four rigs, one
mayor, one scaled `bd.dog` pool. Related: #6122 (retry storm a failing start
produces), #6107 (ephemeral workers never stopped).

title: bug: gc doctor omits effective city suspension from health diagnostics
body:
### Before you continue

- [x] I searched existing issues and did not find an exact duplicate.
- [x] I read the relevant CLI documentation and suspension-state implementation.

### Gas City version

Observed with `gc version --long`: `dev (commit: 11a5dd9d2, built: 2026-09-01T00:17:56-07:00)`.

Also inspected the current upstream `cmd/gc/cmd_doctor.go` on September 7: it registers a legacy suspended-field check and uses effective rig suspension for some checks, but I did not find an effective city-suspension diagnostic. The live reproduction below is on the stated development build, not a claim that I tested a fresh build of upstream main.

### Environment

macOS, zsh, native shared supervisor, tmux runtime, one city with an `od` rig. Database and controller checks pass. No containers are involved.

### Reproduction

Observed on an existing city configured with:

```toml
[workspace]
suspended_on_start = true
```

There is no `.gc/runtime/suspension-state.json` override in this city. The implementation's `EffectiveCitySuspended` uses the runtime override when present, otherwise this configured default.

Run these non-mutating diagnostics against that same city:

```sh
gc --city "$CITY" status --json
gc --city "$CITY" doctor
```

### Expected behavior

Doctor should visibly report effective city suspension and explain that agent work is intentionally paused even when infrastructure is healthy. An informational result or advisory is appropriate; suspension alone need not fail the command.

Ideally the result distinguishes a runtime override from the configured startup default, uses the same suspension resolution as the runtime, and points to inspection/resume documentation without automatically resuming anything. An unreadable suspension state should be reported as unknown rather than inferred to be running.

### Actual behavior

Status reports suspension, but doctor emits no equivalent city-level explanation. Its controller and database checks pass. Someone using doctor to understand why the city does no work can miss the top-level condition preventing agent execution.

### Logs, screenshots, or traces

Relevant status fields:

```json
{
  "suspended": true,
  "health": {
    "usable": false,
    "degraded": true,
    "signals": ["city_suspended", "no_agents_running"]
  }
}
```

The status response was cached (about 162 seconds old at the final evidence read). The current on-disk startup default and absence of a runtime override independently agree with it; the status cache is not presented as an uncached live probe.

Relevant doctor output:

```text
✓ expanded-config-load — expanded config loaded
✓ config-valid — agents, rigs, and services valid
✓ legacy-suspended-field — no deprecated suspended fields in city.toml
✓ controller — controller running (sessions managed)
✓ beads-store — store accessible
✓ dolt-server — reachable on 127.0.0.1:14469
✗ order-firing-current — scheduled orders are stale
85 passed, 2 warnings, 1 failed
```

Neither warning explains effective city suspension. They concern local provider readiness and config semantics. No resume or fix command was run for this reproduction.

### Additional context

Related but distinct:

- #5742 concerns missing required runtimes for unsuspended always-mode sessions while the controller runs.
- #2725, #5268, and #5270 concern suspended-rig order freshness and its source of suspension state.
- #5575 concerns preserving historical stall evidence across suspension intervals.

This report asks for visibility of effective city suspension. It does **not** assert that every stale order in a suspended city is a false positive, request suppressing historical failures, or propose automatic resume. Any change to order eligibility/freshness should be evaluated separately.

title: Design check: per-agent sort policy for the hook's routed first-row claim (oldest-first since #2800 ignores priority)
body:
### What

`gc hook --claim`'s routed first-row tier (`internal/config/workquery.go`, `routedReadyTierCommand`) asks bd for `--sort oldest --limit=20`, and the hook claims the first claimable row in that order. A bead's priority is never consulted at dequeue. #2800 introduced oldest-first deliberately; the PR body gives the ordering itself and no further rationale.

### Where it bites

A city that raises a bead to P0 to expedite it (a review pipeline lifting a labelled PR's review beads) sees the pool keep claiming the oldest unclaimed root regardless. Measured on one city on 2026-09-05: four consecutive orchestrator claims (10:48, 11:49, 12:05, 12:14Z) each took the oldest root, twice passing P0 first-steps for a P2 one; the reviewer pool did the same.

The only knob today is a custom `work_query`, which `EffectiveWorkQuery` returns as the caller-owned full discovery contract — it replaces the crash-recovery, assigned-ready and routed tiers, the federated reader and the held-candidate fail-open — so a pack cannot change the sort alone.

### Proposal, for direction before a PR

A per-agent (or per-pool) routed-tier sort policy, e.g. `routed_sort = "oldest" | "priority" | "hybrid"`, threaded into `routedReadyTierCommand`, default `"oldest"` so current behaviour and #2800's tests stand. bd's own policies at the pinned version: `priority` is priority-then-age within a band (FIFO among equals, a raised priority means something), `hybrid` is created-within-48h by priority then age, `oldest` is pure age. The reconciler's demand count (`PoolDemandServeRules`) is set-based and order-free, so spawn decisions do not change with the sort.

Two questions: (1) is a per-agent field the shape you want, or a `[pool]`-level one; (2) is there a reason oldest-first must stay the only policy that #2800 did not write down (a starvation incident, a determinism requirement across seats)? If the direction is yes, the PR is one config field wired through `AgentPatch`/`AgentOverride`/`Clone`, one token in the tier command, and a workquery golden test.

title: runtime: add bounded liveness observation
body:
## What this changes

This adds an additive runtime helper that reports both liveness and whether the observation completed reliably within a caller-supplied timeout. Callers can now distinguish confirmed absence from an observation that was incomplete because the runtime was unavailable or the deadline expired.

Runtime providers may opt into richer, error-bearing liveness observation. Existing providers retain their current plain-boolean behavior through a compatibility fallback.

## Review notes

- The new surface is `ObservationStatus`, `BoundedLivenessObserver`, and `ObserveLivenessBounded` in `internal/runtime`.
- A deadline returns zero liveness with `Incomplete`; `ErrRuntimeUnavailable` preserves any partial liveness with `Incomplete`; other completed observations remain `Complete`.
- Existing call sites are unchanged. This is groundwork for consumers that need bounded, tri-state observation.
- The timeout bounds the caller's wait. A provider goroutine that ignores cancellation may outlive the call, matching the package's established bounded-observation trade-off.

## Test plan

- [x] Run the full sharded local suite with container-backed tests enabled (`make test-local-full-parallel`).
- [x] Run policy, build, vet, formatting, and lint lanes; attribute reproduced baseline-only failures in the gate record.
- [x] Exercise compatibility fallback, richer observers, unavailable runtime, non-runtime errors, and deadline expiry.
